The Bureaucracy The municipal administration is the second component in the machinery of local government. Often referred to as the bureaucracy, this group includes all municipal staff and senior officials who are employed by the municipality. Kernaghan and Siegel define bureaucracy as a form of organization characterized by hierarchical structure, unity of command, hiring and promotion by merit, and specialization of labour . The term bureaucracy can sometimes have a negative connotation that brings to mind images about inefficient public sector employees. It is, however, based on sound principles of public administration and was introduced in an effort to establish fair and consistent decision-making and service and an emphasis on effectiveness. As Tindal . note, there have traditionally been requirements for the establishment of certain statutory officers of the municipality such as treasurer, clerk, or solicitor . While this has been changing over time and there is significant variation across the country, municipalities tend to have some designated, statutory positions. Municipalities are organized based on five basic models of municipal administration: 1. the departmental model, 2. the commissioner or board of management model, 3. the council-manager model, 4. the manager model, and 5. the city manager model. : Early Models Departmental and Board of Management The relationship between council, the administration, and special purpose bodies has evolved over time. The first period of development was from WWII to the 1970s and was characterized by a high degree of integration between municipal councils and the administration. The departmental model and board of management system were prevalent. Special purpose bodies were generally unquestioned. Departmental Model The departmental model was prominent in Canadian municipalities until the mid-1970s. functions and assigned responsibility for a function to an administrative department head. All department heads reported directly to the municipal council, often through a standing committee. Department heads were equal, and each had an independent relationship with the municipal council. Not surprisingly, the model had the tendency to promote the development of bureaucratic empires within departments. Coordination between departments was weak and there was little incentive to integrate policies or services. Commissioner or Board of Management Model The commissioner or board of management model assigns responsibility for the management of the municipality s affairs to a group or board rather than a single city manager. Each commissioner would have responsibility for a group of services for example, all hard services, soft services, corporate administrative services, etc. The group of commissioners, led by the chief administrative officer as a first among equals, would meet regularly to plan and coordinate the operations and management of the municipality. In the past, the mayor may have participated on the board of commissioners or board of management, providing a political- administrative link. 1970s Onward Shifting Models of Administration from the 1970s Onward By the mid-1970s and into the 1980s there was a shift to CAO and city manager models in larger cities. This changed the relationship between senior staff and elected representatives and between departments, which were under pressure to become more administratively integrated and work horizontally across boundaries. In some areas, there was a questioning of the role of special purpose bodies. The 1990s were a time of re-examination in local government that included looking at who does what, examining how it is done, as well as measuring and reorganizing in an effort to find cost savings and efficiencies. Both of these periods of change were influenced by business approaches and principles. There was a sense that governments in general, and local government in particular, were getting too large, were inefficient in delivering services, and had weak internal controls. Tindal . discuss the influence of new public management in local government in Canada and its influence on the organization of local governments. The emphasis on performance and accountability sets these NPM reforms apart from earlier structural changes, and the use of special purpose bodies and board of management and city manager terminology reinforce the desire for more control over government. Municipalities have continued to adapt to ongoing fiscal, downloading, and political pressures by restructuring and refocusing. In general, there has been a reduction in the number of senior officials in municipalities and an emphasis on integration and horizontal linkages within program areas. Municipal administrations are becoming more dynamic, and new approaches to managing issues are being implemented, including service clusters and project teams that involve internal and external stakeholders. Council-Manager Model The council-manager model, popular in the U.S., shifted power from department heads to a strong, central city manager (also called CAO). In this model, the city manager is the only point of contact for the administration with the elected council. Councils in the city-manager system do not usually have standing committees and there is little no interaction between senior staff and councillors. The manager has authority to hire and fire senior staff and exercises strong control over the administration. The city manager also has significant influence over the council, which does not generally have strong operational or program knowledge. While the city manager or CAO is very powerful, they are also very vulnerable, especially in situations of conflict. Sancton notes that there is no Canadian municipality where the full city manager CAO model has been implemented. Many municipalities were reluctant to move to the city manager model because of a fear that the city manager position would be too powerful both in the internal administrative side of the organization and politically in terms of challenges and rivalries with the mayor and members of council. However, Canadian municipalities faced pressures for greater professionalization and a stronger non-political role in managing the municipality. Thus, a modified manager model has become popular. A professional city manager would oversee all administrative activities and departmental functions and report to the municipal council. While the department heads report to the city manager, they also connect with the council through a standing committee structure and have accountability to council through that committee. Council is responsible for hiring the manager and is generally involved in some way in the appointment of senior staff. Chief Administrative Officer Model The chief administrative officer model is a weak or modified form of the city manager model. The CAO would have responsibility for all the administrative areas in the municipality, including finance, clerks, communications, human resources, and legal, but generally, they did not have responsibility for the operating departments that provide services directly to the public. In this model, these departments, such as parks and recreation, transportation, and social services, would be run by a department head or commissioner who would report directly The CAO would not have responsibility or authority for the major services provided by the municipality. City Manager Model In the city manager model, the most senior municipal staff position is the city manager who has responsibility for all municipal administration and service delivery. The city manager reports directly to council. Many authors, including the authors of the course textbook, will use city manager and chief administrative officer interchangeably. It is important to note that there was and still remains a difference in the roles and scope of authority in some municipalities. Preferred Administration Model Today Most municipalities use some form of the city manager or chief administrative officer. This super-bureaucrat plays a key role in the municipal administration and is usually selected and appointed under contract by the municipal council. what the municipality is looking for in its recruitment for a new CAO. Depending on the individual, they may have different types of relationships with the senior staff department heads. Plunkett (as referenced in Tindal ., 2017, 257) describes three types of relationships: Passive the city manager plays a passive role, coordinating and supporting department heads Dominant the manager plays a dominant role, managing and controlling operations and budgets and policy and program recommendations to council Active active relationships are the third type of relationship and are the most common. The city manager will be actively involved with departments in working toward shared priorities and managing the relationship with council. The city manager or CAO has a tough job navigating between the political and administrative and faces high expectations. As described by Canadian CAOs: The CAO is the conduit between governance and employees having that sensibility around making the politics work and the business work. (StrategyCorp, 2019, 53) Being a CAO is about knowing how to live in the political world while keeping one foot firmly in the administrative world. (StrategyCorp, 2018, 36) Municipal issues are complex and interconnected, and there is constant pressure for both innovation and efficiency. Municipalities provide services directly, but they also must manage services that are contracted out or delivered through private-public partnerships or other partnership arrangements. The municipal environment is dynamic because there are multiple stakeholders with competing interests, including the public, property owners (and taxpayers), businesses, developers, nonprofits and charities, the province or territory, and the federal government. Expectations are high. Bureaucratic Influence Bureaucrats are expected to be unbiased, objective, and nonpartisan. Nonetheless, by virtue of their position, expertise, and experience, they exert varying degrees of influence on what municipal government does and how it is done. Senior officials have the most significant influence. While elected members of council vote on policies and programs, the senior bureaucrat plays a critical role in advising the members and implementing their decisions. reports to the standing committees (and sometimes directly to council) about issues, programs, funding, or new policies. Sometimes they are asked by these committees or by council to prepare a report on an issue; other times, they take the initiative and propose a new program or policy or a change to an existing policy. They answer questions, provide information at the committee meeting, and explain why they feel the item should be approved. Once a decision has been made, they are responsible for implementing the decision. There is usually some discretion involved in implementation or policy enforcement, and the senior staff can influence the implementation. Elected councillors rely heavily on senior staff. Councillors are often part-time and rarely have the background, education, or experience in the service areas. They are responsible for a wide range of services they cannot be experts in all the service areas and they come to rely on the knowledgeable and experienced senior staff for advice and direction. Often senior staff have an opinion or perspective on the issue, and their advice is influenced by their staff s perspective on the issue. The non-parliamentary nature of council politics reinforces the influence of the bureaucracy. Political parties usually develop position statements on key policy issues these statements guide the politicians while in office. When they are elected, their platform provides guidance to the bureaucrats concerning priorities and policy directions. As previously discussed, there is no formal party politics at the municipal level, and the municipal election does not create a clear mandate for staff to follow. This discussion is not meant to suggest that senior bureaucrats run the show at municipal council. Rather, it is to illustrate their influence on the machinery of local government and decision-making processes. Accountability Structures and Officers Municipalities may also include one or more independent accountability officers. These roles have been added by municipal councils over the last 20 years as independent officers reporting directly to council. While these officers are employees of the municipality, they are not part of the bureaucracy or administration. They instead focus on distinct functions related to accountability integrity; ethics; complaints; lobbying; stewardship of resources; and open, accessible decision-making. A municipal government must act in the best interest of its community members. councillors are elected by voters and are accountable and responsive to them. But elections are every four years, and accountability is muddied by factors such as poor memory; lack of information; fragmented service and funding structures and program partnerships; and contracting out. We will explore issues of municipal accountability later in the Module 10 discussion of municipal relationships with the public. In addition to accountability through elections, some provinces and territories have provided the option in provincial municipal acts for municipalities to pass bylaws to add formal accountability functions to their municipality. For example, the 2 Ontario Municipal Act gave municipalities the authority to appoint accountability officers. In other cases, provinces have required municipalities to add or arrange for specific accountability functions. Some of the specific accountability functions are described in the following tabs and include: : Integrity Commissioner Integrity commissioners are concerned with the ethical behaviour of elected councillors and the mayor, administer the code of conduct, and provide advice to members of council about potential conflict of interest or ethical issues. Integrity commissioners have authority over municipal councils and municipal agencies, boards, and commissions. Did You Know? Toronto created the first full-time municipal integrity commissioner in 2004 following the Bellamy Inquiry into a computer leasing scandal, which is discussed in the readings for this week. Calgary appointed an integrity commissioner in 2016 with dual integrity and ethics advisory responsibility. A municipal ombudsman is an independent officer who reviews actions and decisions taken by municipal councils and their agencies, boards, and commissions. Ombudsman functions have authority to investigate complaints from the public and to initiate investigations when they feel they are warranted. The exceptions are policy decisions and financial matters (which are the responsibility of the auditor general). The City of Montreal established an ombudsman in 2002. Ontario municipalities can establish their own independent officers or choose to be covered by the Ontario ombudsman. The Ontario ombudsman has authority to review decisions of municipal ombudspersons, except for those of the Toronto officer. Halifax, Winnipeg, and Vancouver are required to have ombudsman functions by their respective provincial legislation. Auditor General A municipal auditor general is different from the internally focused municipal auditor that is part of the municipal administration and reports through a committee of council. The independent auditor general reports directly to council and helps municipal councils be accountable for the stewardship of public funds and resources. Toronto is the only Ontario municipality required, in the 2 City of Toronto Act, to have an independent auditor general. Some municipalities have moved to integrate the auditor general and internal audit functions: Winnipeg changed the responsibilities for their auditor general to include internal audit functions in 2009 as have Hamilton, Calgary, and Edmonton. British Columbia appointed a provincial auditor general in 2012 to provide the independent review function for municipalities in that province. Lobbyist Registrar Registration A lobbyist registration system requires lobbyists to register with the municipality and to comply with municipal rules, processes, and codes of conduct. Lobbyists generally must register each interaction with municipal representatives, identifying who they lobbied and why. The cities of Toronto and Hamilton have independent lobbyist registrars with responsibility for administering the process. When it was set up, Toronto s lobbyist registration was voluntary, but it was subsequently changed to mandatory. The City of Ottawa has combined the integrity commissioner and lobbyist registrar function. The City of Winnipeg originally established an integrity commissioner but expanded the role to include lobbyist registrar before the first official was appointed in early 2017. Closed Meeting Investigator Municipal acts use terms like open, transparent, and accountable to describe municipal decision-making processes. This legislation sets out strict parameters for municipalities to meet in camera in meetings that are closed to the public. The closed meeting investigator reviews municipalities to ensure that they are functioning in accordance with the closed meeting rules. The British Columbia provincial ombudsman investigates closed municipal meetings; in Ontario, the provincial ombudsman does the same, except for Toronto and Ottawa, which have independent closed meeting investigators. Accountability officers provide advice and make recommendations to municipal councils, who, in turn, have the authority to make decisions on the issues and impose any penalties or sanctions. Accountability officers have limited formal authority, but considerable power to influence public opinion (Sancton, 2017, 1). Their independence and public reports provide valuable information to municipal voters and community members. Pause and Reflect Examine your municipalities website. Does it talk about accountability to the community and voters? Does the municipality have accountability officers? If not, does it provide information for community members about how to access provincial officers who provide oversight on municipal decisions and actions? Is the information easy to find and clearly communicated? Do a bit more digging to learn if your municipality has had issues related to accountability. If so, what role did accountability officers play in investigating and resolving the issue? What Are Special Purpose Bodies and What Do They Do? In addition to municipalities, there are a number of other decision-making service delivery bodies at the municipal level known as special purpose bodies or agencies, boards, and commissions that are part of local government. Tindal . estimate that there are about 8,000 municipal special purpose bodies in Canada that control significant resources. I n many Canadian cities, more than a third of the city s operating budget is handed over to special-purpose bodies every year. (Lucas, 2013, 2) Examples include transit commissions, police services boards, hydro commissions, heritage boards, and conservation authorities. Key Point Special purpose bodies are assigned specific responsibility for a purpose or mandate; their role and powers vary depending on their area of focus. These bodies differ greatly in their role and membership. Some have service delivery responsibility while others have service delivery and policy-making powers. Special purpose bodies generally have jurisdictional boundaries that reflect municipal boundaries or the boundaries of a group of municipalities. They have a degree of autonomy from the municipal government and can be created by municipal bylaw or imposed by a province or territory through legislation. Agencies, boards, and commissions are controlled by independent boards that include elected municipal representatives, municipal appointees, provincial appointees, or a mix of each. Funding arrangements also vary they can t impose taxes and often impose user charges. They may receive significant funding from the municipal government or provincial grants. In some cases the municipality will have authority to approve the agency, board, or commission budget because it is integrated into the municipal budget; in other cases it can either approve or reject (but not adjust) the budget; and in other cases, it has no control over the budget. Why Do We Have Special Purpose Bodies? During the early reform phases (discussed in Module 2), provinces deliberately established municipal special purpose bodies to transfer power away from the municipalities to bodies that were composed of provincial appointees (e.g., the Ontario Railway and Municipal Board established in 1906). This served to undermine local democracy by taking power from locally elected representatives and giving it to provincially appointed individuals. In 1977, John Robarts, previous premier of Ontario, headed up a royal commission reviewing the municipal government in the city of Toronto s two-tier metro system. Robarts wrote: The province exercises control over many local services by delegating the responsibility for them not to councils but to special purpose bodies and further that they appear to be sub- units of provincial administration rather than units of local government administration (Ontario, 1977, 96 and 99). This tension continues with each appointment to a provincially designated municipal special purpose body. Provincially established special purpose bodies still serve to disperse decision-making about municipal services and weaken municipal councils. Municipalities have established special purpose bodies, most recently as part of new public management initiatives to move municipalities out of the business of and position them as policy makers, steering the municipality. Municipalities established new corporations and delegated responsibility to them for programs, and they established new bodies with other municipalities to manage joint programs. Municipal special purpose bodies are established by municipalities to serve municipal interests. Many of these organizations are formally incorporated, like the Toronto Transit Commission , Toronto Community Housing, and the Toronto Zoo. The municipality is the sole shareholder of the organization and sets the terms, conditions, and mandate for the special purpose body. Ontario municipalities have a number of other municipal bodies, established in response to provincial legislation and requirements, that vary in the level of control and influence in the municipality. For example, school boards are directly funded by and accountable to the Ontario government, yet school board representatives are directly elected in municipal elections. Police service boards and public health boards include some municipally elected representatives and appointed citizen members. Police boards also include provincially appointed members. Inter-municipal Agencies, Boards, or Commissions Sometimes municipalities work together to form organizations like the Association of Municipalities of Ontario , the Association of Manitoba Municipalities , or the Federation of Municipalities of Canada . Alternatively, they may collaborate with municipal neighbours by establishing an agency to address issues of joint concern. Provincially Established Municipal Special Purpose Bodies Many special purpose bodies are mandated by the province or territory. This means that there is legislation that assigns responsibility for the service to an agency, board, or commission established by the province or territory. Here are three Ontario-based examples to illustrate different types of provincially established municipal special purpose bodies. : Police Services Boards Ontario In Ontario, the Police Services Act requires the establishment of a police services board in every municipality that has a police force. The legislation describes the role, membership, and appointment of local police services boards. Boards of three, five, or seven members are required, depending on population size. The police services board in Toronto includes the mayor, two councillors, three provincial appointees, and one citizen appointee. The police chief is accountable to the board, and the board is accountable to the community as well as to the Ontario Civilian In 2019, the City of Toronto estimated that the average property owner, with a property tax of 3,020, would contribute 703.21 toward the cost of policing . Even though the City of Toronto has to raise the money to pay for policing through the property tax, they do not direct the police force or set policing policy, with three of seven votes on the police services board. Metrolinx Metrolinx is a provincial agency that was originally established as the Greater Toronto Transit Authority and included members from municipal councils in the Greater Toronto area. The GTTA was changed to Metrolinx in 2006 and given responsibility for regional transportation planning, developing a unified regional transit fare system, procurement, and duties including development and construction related to the regional transportation system. Metrolinx s 15-member board of directors is appointed by the Lieutenant Governor of Ontario on behalf of Ontario. There are no elected members of council from any of the municipalities in the Metrolinx catchment area on the board of directors, even though some of them operate municipal transit programs. The provincial agency makes decisions that have implications for municipal transit operators. For example, Metrolinx is rolling out a common electronic payment system, called Presto, across the partner transit systems. Each transit operator is concerned about a negative impact of this system on their operations. The TTC, Toronto s transit provider, published the results of a study that the TTC had lost revenues of about 4.2 M as a result of the Toronto roll-out of the payment system. In addition, Metrolinx s responsibility for transit planning and decisions about investment in new transit have implications for municipal economic development and growth. Decisions about new GO stations (a regional transit service) or frequency of transit service can influence the shape of municipalities. Metrolinx provides an example of a provincially established ABC that integrates and plans for regions (including municipalities) without decision-making involvement of the elected officials from those municipalities. You have read about the Ontario Municipal Board in earlier modules. Other provinces have similar independent oversight bodies established to monitor and make some decisions related to municipalities. The OMB was established in 1906 as the Ontario Railway and Municipal Board to oversee the finances of municipalities and supervise the railways, which were, at the time, the main source of transport between municipalities. Eventually, the OMB gained more responsibility to adjudicate in cases of dispute related to some regulations, planning, and development. Interestingly, it has retained authority to approve municipal borrowing for capital expenditures for all Ontario municipalities! The OMB was controversial in its role as the appeal body in the case of a dispute over a municipal decision. It was used most frequently to challenge decisions regarding zoning and planning matters, but Module 4 described how a councillor appealed to the OMB regarding the decision on Toronto ward boundaries. In 2018, Ontario replaced the OMB by giving municipalities the authority to establish independent local planning appeal tribunals in accordance with provincial legislation. Toronto set up a Toronto Local Planning Appeal Tribunal to assume some of the functions previously provided by the OMB, including appeals on a range of planning and land matters. In 2019, Ontario announced changes to the LPAT process instead of referring appeals back to the municipality for further consideration if the tribunal disagreed with the municipal decision, the LPAT would have the authority to make the final and binding decision. In effect, they were given the powers of the old OMB, which led to widespread criticism of that provincial agency. This is a good example of how agencies can be used and adapted based on political interests in this case, based on provincial interests. Are Special Purpose Bodies Good for Local Government? There is considerable debate whether special purpose bodies are good for local government. Supporters argue that some services, such as policing, may be too sensitive to leave in the hands of elected officials and they appreciate the mixed board structure that includes at least one community representative. Others support the focus and attention to a service area or issue given by a special purpose body and to the assignment of responsibility to appointees with expertise and knowledge of the issue area. Municipalities have wide and broad responsibility. Assigning some of that responsibility to a special purpose agency will bring attention and clear focus to that service and, at the same time, will give municipal councils more time and energy to address their core functions. The result may be more effective and more efficient service delivery. Critics counter that it is undemocratic to take power from elected officials who have been chosen by the public to represent them and assign it to appointed individuals with no direct accountability. Unelected special purpose bodies may not be responsive to public concerns. The existence of so many bodies can lead to confusion among residents about how local government works. Transparency in decision-making processes may vary among municipal agencies, contributing to confusion and concerns about accountability. Similar questions of accountability can be directed to the composition of the boards. Should they include elected or appointed members or both? What about provincial boards established in municipal areas should they include municipal representatives, either elected or appointed? Accountability is also important in funding. Municipalities contribute to many agencies, boards, and commissions but don t always have a say in how the resources are used. Provincially established municipal agencies bring additional benefits and challenges. If the agency crosses municipal boundaries, it has potential to bring attention and leadership to a shared issue of concern. It is possible that a provincially established municipal agency will have access to provincial funds that otherwise wouldn t have been available. Moreover, in situations where there is conflict among municipalities, a provincially established municipal agency may be able to negotiate a resolution. Provincial special purpose bodies are often seen to be a way of weakening local councils and extending provincial control This happens through the establishment of the agency and in the ongoing appointment of provincial nominees to the board of the special purpose body. There is no local accountability for the actions of provincial municipal agencies the accountability is to the province. Community members, confused by municipal agencies and the municipality, will be further confused by the existence of provincially established agencies at the municipal level. As the examples showed, there is potential for conflict and tension about political agendas and priorities and funding. Provincially established municipal agencies reduce scope for municipal decision-making autonomy John Robarts, quoted earlier, recommended that all special purpose bodies be abolished and that responsibility for the issue areas should be given back to municipalities. Pause and Reflect Look again at your municipal website. Does the website identify any municipally established special purpose bodies? If so, what do they do and how do they connect with the municipality? Are there some agencies, boards, and commissions that you know about that aren t listed on the website? Why? What about provincial special purpose bodies? Is there information on the municipal website about them? If not, is it easy to identify them and learn more? Finally, do you think there are more advantages or disadvantages to having municipal special purpose bodies? What about provincially established municipal agencies, boards, and commissions are you pro or con? Summary This module completes our look at the machinery of local government. It showed that municipal councils may be the elected decision-makers in local government, but agencies, boards, and commissions also make important decisions about key municipal services and programs. The module distinguished between municipally and provincially established special purpose bodies that are active at the municipal level and considered the implications for municipal authority and autonomy. Staff support informed decision-making and implement directions from council they too play an important role in shaping and influencing decisions and implementation. The different administrative models show different relationships between senior staff and municipal councils, with implications for authority and influence. The module introduced accountability officers senior staff appointed directly by municipal council who report directly to council. These accountability officers are independent municipal employees and are not part of the administration. Not all municipalities have these functions, but many are covered by officers providing some of the functions at the provincial or territorial level. The machinery of local government is complex and dynamic. It changes over time based on events and actions, our understanding of local government, and the relationships between the elected representatives, the administration, and the agencies, boards, and commissions. The assignment Municipal Decision-Making due at the end of this course week will give you the opportunity to further reflect on the machinery of local government. The municipal administration is a key element of the machinery of local government. The administrative models have evolved over time based on a number of pressures, including the relationship with council. Most municipalities follow a city manager (or CAO) model. The city manager plays an important leadership role in the municipality, straddling the political and administrative and juggling a range of challenging issues. Municipal accountability functions include integrity commissioners, municipal ombudspersons, auditor generals, lobbyist registrars, and closed meeting investigators. These may be internal to the municipality, reporting directly to council and separate from municipal administrations, or provided by the province or territory for all municipalities. Municipal agencies, boards, and commissions play important roles in delivering a range of local services and programs. They can be established by the municipality or by a province or territory to cover one or more municipalities. While there are clear benefits to special purpose bodies, there are also some important challenges related to accountability, transparency, and autonomy. The Machinery of Municipal Government Before venturing into the larger and less distinct world of local gover- nance, let s begin with the machinery of local government. More spe- cifically, we will examine the machinery of municipal government not including the structures that may be found amongst the wide variety of agencies, boards, and commissions that form part of local government. On the surface, this approach sounds quite straightforward, and the basic structure of municipal government is certainly simpler than that found at the provincial and federal levels, with their separate executive and legislative branches. There aren t separate branches of government at the municipal level; responsibilities are concentrated in the elected council and are carried out by appointed staff who are mostly organized into a number of functionally specialized departments. he powers assigned to a municipality are exercised on behalf of its resi- dents and ratepayers by a council elected by them. Provincial legislation usually includes provisions for the form of council and such details as the number of councillors and whether election is by general vote (at-large) or by ward (a distinction discussed below). legislation passed in most provinces over the past decade (and discussed in Chapter 6) often gives municipalities somewhat more discretion with respect to such matters. Municipal councils consist of a head (known as warden or chair in counties and other upper-tier governments; mayor in cities and towns; and reeve, chair, or overseer in villages and townships) and a widely varying number of councillors. While the total membership varies greatly, there has been a tendency to have small councils of from 5 to 15 members, largely on the grounds that a small group is less unwieldy and more efficient in making decisions with the more recent exceptions being amalgamated megacities such as Toronto. Members of council are expected to represent the local community and act on its behalf although that role is not nearly as simple or straightforward as it sounds, as discussed below. They also exercise a policy-making role through which they determine services and service levels, approve budgets, enact rules and regulations, and generally shape the local community and the quality of life within it. A third general role of councillors is managerial (for want of a better term), and it involves Chapter 8 Municipal Governing Structures 227 providing an oversight of municipal operations to ensure that policies are implemented as intended, funds are expended as authorized, and pro- grams are delivered efficiently and effectively. This local politician civic staff relationship is sometimes a bit more nuanced, with suggestions that permanent professional staff can at times have more policy sway than is generally understood.5 THE REPRESENTATIVE ROLE OF MEMBERS OF COUNCIL The roles of councillors in making policy and overseeing implementation of policy by municipal staff receive a good deal of emphasis and will be explored in a subsequent section on council-staff relations. But it is a con- sistent theme of this text that the representative role of municipal govern- ment is most important, and it is the elected members of council who fulfill this role, well or poorly. The longstanding bias in favour of small councils makes it more likely that they will not represent adequately the diversity of the population. Relatively small councils are even found in many of Canada s largest municipalities. While First Nations, M tis, and Inuit are legally recognized as Aboriginal in the Constitution Act, 1982, this wasn t always the case. There were past legal distinctions between the three groups and for many years Indian peoples were the only peoples formally recognized in the Constitution. A Supreme Court ruling in 1929 recognized Inuit peoples as covered by the Constitution Act, 1987 (OECD, 2020, 44). M tis were legally recognized for the first time in the Constitution Act, 1982 (OECD, 2020, 44). Colonial Settlements and Land This module is about the relationship that municipalities have with Indigenous peoples and communities. It is hard to know where to start this module because there is much history and practice that informs how we got to the place that we are at today. We will be guided by our focus on relationships between municipalities local government and Indigenous peoples. The module content will highlight past actions and current practices that are relevant to that relationship, but it does not provide a fulsome discussion of the relationship that non-Indigenous people and their institutions have with Indigenous peoples. You are strongly encouraged to continue to learn about these historical relationships to round out the condensed history that is included in this module. Historical Events Did You Know? Review this timeline of key historical events and or interactions between Indigenous and non- Indigenous peoples in Canada. Source extracted from Reconciliation with Indigenous Peoples: A Holistic Approach Other than the remains of a Viking presence in L Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland as early as the 8th century, John Cabot is credited as the first European to set foot on the land we now call Canada in 1497, in an area that had previously been settled by Indigenous peoples. Cabot was followed by other Europeans, primarily from England and France, and over time they established settlements or colonies. These settlements grew over time and tensions arose between the two groups of settlers the English and French. Following a loss in the Seven Years War, France gave up their claim and control of land in Canada to Britain. The King of England issued a Royal Proclamation in 1783 that is sometimes referred to as the Indigenous Magna Carta of Canada , which proclaimed the land as British. Importantly, the Proclamation also recognized the rights of Indigenous peoples and outlined a treaty process through which Indigenous land could be legally ceded to the Crown. The best places for settlements involved lands that were near waterways for transportation, were good for growing crops, and could be protected against military action. These were lands already occupied by Indigenous peoples, but over time and as settlements grew, the colonists began to dislocate the Indigenous peoples. For example, the M tis were moved away by treaty from the Red River area . Despite the vision set out by the Royal Proclamation, the rapid influx of settlers, commercial development of natural resources, the arrival of European forms of governance and political expediency soon eroded the land base and livelihood of Indigenous peoples . As we know today, there are many examples that indicate that treaties were not fairly negotiated or properly executed by the colonists. Did You Know? The Toronto Purchase, 1787 (amended in 1805), involved the transfer of land of the Mississaugas of the New Credit First Nation to the Crown. Many questions were raised over the subsequent years about the treaty, which was very unclear on the land involved and whether the chiefs had actually agreed to the treaty. More than two hundred years later, a land claim was made and in 2010 a settlement was reached between the Crown and the Mississaugas of the New Credit. The Foundations for the Relationship The Constitution Act, 1867 is critical to understanding the context for today s relationships between municipalities and Indigenous peoples. It gave the federal government jurisdiction over Indians (the term used in the Constitution) and over lands reserved for Indians (Graham and Peters, 2002, 5) and recognized the treaty system and related commitments to Indians. As we know, the Constitution also gave provinces the jurisdiction to establish local governments, which they would control. Did You Know? The Constitution Act was followed by the Indian Act, 1876, which established the rules and process for determining Indian status and the division of responsibility for Indians between the federal and provincial territorial governments. of the Indian Act assigns responsibilities, similar to those assigned by provinces to municipalities, to elected Band Councils; while Section 82(2) gives the federal minister the authority to overrule a bylaw or decision taken by a Band Council, similar to the override that provinces have of municipal decisions. Band councils were imposed on Indigenous peoples by the Government of Canada to eradicate the hereditary system of governance and create something more recognizable for the western government . Band councils included an elected chief and elected council members and had delegated authority for the designed reserve. The hereditary system, based on representation from clans and involvement of elders, represents more traditional leadership. Hereditary chiefs are seen as traditional knowledge keepers, and in some contexts are recognized as having greater authority and rights relative to things like traditional territory or cultural knowledge and tradition . Recent disputes about the Coastal GasLink pipeline have highlighted the differences between the two forms of governance one imposed and elected and the other traditional and hereditary. The Indian Act was amended in 1951 to transfer responsibility for M tis, non-status Indians, and off- reserve Indigenous peoples to the provinces, while the federal government retained responsibility for Indigenous peoples living on reserve. Know the Act . Paikin interviews Bob Joseph about the book 2 Things You May Not Know About The Indian Act: Helping Canadians Make Reconciliation with Indigenous Peoples a Reality. The video provides an overview of this legislation and provides insight on how it continues to shape relationships today. Shifting Responsibility As you remember from earlier modules, urbanization was a strong force beginning in the 1950s, and Indigenous peoples were part of this trend. In 1959, 17 of registered Indians lived off reserve; by 1996 this had increased to 42 (Ontario, 2009, 602). Urbanization served to shift responsibility from the federal government to the provinces (as a result of the 1951 amendment to the Indian Act) and the result was a gap in policy while the Indian Act didn t apply, there was no, or very limited, provincial legislation or policy framework to take its place in Ontario or other provinces. The Constitution Act was patriated in 1982 and included formal recognition of Aboriginal and treaty rights. There are two sections of particular relevance to the discussion of the relationship with municipalities: Part 1 Section 25 this section guarantees certain rights and freedoms in the Constitution, regardless of Aboriginal, treaty, or other rights and any rights set out in land claims or other agreements Part 2 Section 35 this section recognizes Indian, Inuit, and M tis people as Aboriginal Peoples of Canada. It recognizes existing Aboriginal and treaty rights, including land claim agreements, and serves to entrench Aboriginal and treaty rights in the Constitution. The changes in the Constitution Act, 1982 provided an opportunity for policy and other changes through courts and policy processes, but it didn t change the status and form of Indigenous governments in Canada (Graham and Peters, 2002, 194). The Indian Act was again amended in 1985. This amendment removed previous restrictions on status so that women who married non-Indigenous persons could apply to be reinstated as status Indians by their band council. Alternatives to the Indian Act Two pieces of legislation offered alternatives to the Indian Act for First Nations governance. First Nations Land Management Act, 1 This legislation delegated some land management responsibilities from the Indian Act to band councils and removed a requirement for approval of land-related decisions by the minister responsible for First Nations. Band councils that met the requirements, including the development of a land code, would assume responsibility for the creation, administration, and enforcement of laws about the management of reserve lands. By October 2019, 7 First Nations had developed the required land code, between 10 and 15 were in the process of ratifying a code, and 55 were in the process of developing a code (OECD, 2020, 56). The shift to land management is one-way First Nations that move to the Land Management Act cannot choose to return to land management under the Indian Act. First Nations Fiscal Management Act, 2 This legislation gave First Nations jurisdiction over a number of core government functions as well as some new revenue tools. As of October 2019, 2 First Nations had opted into the framework and 125 of those had started to collect property tax (OECD, 2020, 56). While these options gave First Nations more responsibility and autonomy, they were both based on the structure of band council governance imposed through the Indian Act. Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples In 1991, Mohawk First Nations people protested the expansion of a golf course and housing development on disputed lands in Kanesatake that included a Mohawk burial ground. The 78-day dispute near the town of Oka was complex and involved many players in this and other communities. As you can tell from the video, the situation was volatile and tense. When it ended, the federal government purchased the land identified for the golf course expansion but has not transferred the land to the Mohawks of Kanesatake as reserve lands (Marshall, 2013 updated by McIntosh and Doerr, 2020). Following the Oka crisis and related protests and resistance across the country, the federal government appointed a Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples in August 1991 to look at the relationship between First Nations, Inuit, M tis peoples and the Government of Canada and Canadian society. The Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples engaged in extensive research and consultations related to governance, land and economy, social and cultural issues, and the North, and produced five reports. The final report, submitted in 1996, included discussions of governance. The commission supported self-governance and estimated that there were 60 to 8 Aboriginal Nations that could be self-governing. The Royal Commission also recommended an Aboriginal parliament to advise parliament on Aboriginal issues and three governance models for Aboriginal peoples living in urban areas. Canada responded with Gathering Strength: Canada s Aboriginal Action Plan that included a commitment to improve services to urban Aboriginal peoples. In 1998, Canada established the Urban Aboriginal Strategy to provide support and funding for the development of community organizations to address the needs of urban Aboriginal peoples in select urban municipalities, and better coordinate and integrate policies at the federal level and with federal partners. The strategy was instrumental in bringing policy actors together (Heritz, 2018, 607). Growing Urban Indigenous Populations At the same time that these formal changes were happening in the relationship between First Nations and the Government of Canada and the provinces, changes were continuing to happen within Indigenous communities. The migration to urban centres put increasing attention on governance and service issues for Aboriginal peoples living in urban areas, while pressure continued for on-reserve First Nation governance and services. Developments at the federal level between government and Indigenous peoples were complemented by efforts at the municipal level. The Centre for Municipal Aboriginal Relations (the Centre) was established in 1996 to promote municipal-Indigenous relations through research about agreements and good relationship practices. In 2001, the Centre formed a committee to focus on collaborative relationships between municipalities and First Nations that were adjacent or close to urban areas. The Federation of Canadian Municipalities partnered with the Department of Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Canada to establish the First Nations-Municipal Community Infrastructure Partnership program. The program made resources and funding available for hard and soft infrastructure through municipal-First Nations partnerships. Truth and Reconciliation Commission The Truth and Reconciliation Commission was established to determine the truth about residential schools and lay the foundation for the important question of reconciliation . Reconciliation was defined as establishing and maintaining a mutually respectful relationship between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal peoples in this country . The relationship between Indigenous and settler peoples in Canada was one of nations encountering nations, where one gradually oppressed and marginalized the other. Indigenous peoples never agreed to the denial of their sovereignty, cultures or identities. Thus, in the Canadian context, reconciliation must refer to transformative as opposed to restorative reconciliation (Stanton, 2011 as quoted in Vizina and Wilson, 2019, 10). In 2015, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission issued 9 Calls to Action, five of which directly refer to municipalities (bolded below) and seven that refer to government or all levels of government: 3 fully implement Jordan s Principle 17 support residential school survivors and families to reclaim their original names 23 increase number of Aboriginal health care professionals, support retention of Aboriginal health professionals in Aboriginal communities, and provide cultural competency training for all health care professionals 40 establish Indigenous-specific victim programs and services 43 adopt and implement the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples as the framework for reconciliation 47 reject concepts used to justify European sovereignty over Indigenous peoples and land 57 educate municipal public servants and develop skills in intercultural competency, conflict resolution, human rights and anti-racism efforts 64 require denominational schools to provide comparative religious studies including on Indigenous spiritual beliefs and practices 75 protect residential school cemeteries 77 provide records of residential schools to the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation 87 provide public education on the history of Indigenous athletes in Canada 88 take action to support the development of Indigenous athletes Sources: 3, 17 and 23 summarized from the TRC Report; 43, 47, 57, 64, 75, 77, 87, 88 from Vizina and Wilson, 2019, 11. Did You Know? These Calls to Action have implications for the municipalities and their ongoing relationship with Indigenous peoples. The City of Winnipeg established an Indigenous Relations Division in 2013 to coordinate Indigenous-specific programs and initiatives. This division has been given responsibility for the implementation of the TRC Calls to Action. The city has developed Winnipeg s Indigenous Accord and reports annually on their progress. The video Welcoming Winnipeg provides an introduction to the accord. Other initiatives include the Mayor s Indigenous Advisory Circle; an Aboriginal Youth Strategy; an extensive research guide available through Winnipeg Public Library; and Welcoming Winnipeg, an advisory committee of community members. The Winnipeg initiative has also focused on educating and engaging youth. You are encouraged, but not required, to watch the video Educating Our Youth Truth and Reconciliation . Please note that this optional video is not closed captioned. Indigenous Self-Government Canada recognized the inherent right to Indigenous self-government in Section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 and established the Inherent Right Policy in 1995 to guide the self-government negotiations with Indigenous peoples . Self-government agreements are negotiated between Canada and the Indigenous community within the framework of the Constitution and consistent with federal laws. These agreements give Indigenous communities a variety of political and legal powers that are somewhat akin to what provinces and municipalities have (Alcantara and Nelles, 2014, 183). In 2019, there were 25 agreements that involved 4 Indigenous communities, two education self-governance agreements involving 3 Indigenous communities, and negotiations were underway for another 50 agreements . Self- government takes different forms it may be comprehensive or limited to specific services like education. The Modern Treaties and Self-Government Agreements map shows the territory covered by the different agreements. same time, the First Nation became a member of the Metro Vancouver Board a partnership of 21 municipalities, the Tsawwassen First Nation, and one electoral area (Metro Vancouver, 2019). Successful Struggle for Self-Governance . Agreement The earliest self-government agreements were signed in the 1990s in the Yukon. None of the 1 First Nations in the Yukon had signed treaties in the past with the Crown and none of them had reserve lands. These First Nations began negotiating with the federal government in 1973 and the final agreement was approved and ratified in 1994 (Alcantara and Nelles, 2009, 715). This agreement served as the framework agreement that was to be used to negotiate individual agreements that could be tailored with specific provisions to each of the 1 First Nations. The Kwanlin D n First Nation began to negotiate their agreement with the federal government in 1995, but progress stalled until 1999 when a new chief was elected and the negotiations resumed. Three of the outstanding issues in the negotiations had implications for the City of Whitehorse: the inclusion of waterfront lands in the City of Whitehorse as part of the settlement lands owned by the municipality , clarification of the First Nation s self-government powers in the city (that is, land use planning), property taxation exemptions (because all land transferred under a treaty would immediately become taxable and would probably bankrupt Kwanlin Despite the impact on the city of these issues Whitehorse owned the land in question, there was potential for incompatible development and property standards within the urban area, and they were at risk of losing property tax dollars the City of Whitehorse was not allowed to formally participate in the negotiations, which was conducted between the federal and territorial governments. Earlier Whitehorse councils had not been supportive of a land claims agreement, however, with the election of a new mayor and council in 2000, things began to change. In the end, the City of Whitehorse sold the prime waterfront land to the territory, so it could be included in the 2002 self-government agreement. There were various conditions that require the Kwanlin D n to use city bylaws for the lands and a service agreement was negotiated for services that the city would provide to the waterfront land. As Alcantara and Nelles observe in the case study, the ownership of the land was a deal breaker that gave the municipality a powerful veto over negotiations . But the development of the waterfront lands was a priority for the city, and the development by the Kwanlin D n and the construction of a Kwanlin D n cultural centre were not construed as bad outcomes from the city s point of view (Alcantara and Nelles, 2009, 721). The lands would be subject to municipal bylaws and standards, servicing would be provided at cost, and there were benefits from reducing the uncertainty about the implications of the waterfront land claim on the city. The result supported the economic and community goals of Whitehorse. of self-government in the Yukon. This video is not closed captioned; click here for a transcript of the video. Whitehorse has continued to develop respectful and strong relationships with two First Nations. In June Declaration of Commitment that describes collaboration, ongoing communications and respect. Regular meetings are held between the municipal council and each First Nation, and the municipality is taking steps to ensure that municipal staff are aware and informed the municipality requires municipal staff to complete a Yukon First Nations 101 course offered by the local college (Vizina and Wilson, 2019, 28). As you can see from this case study, the negotiation process takes a long time and is complicated by changing leadership, and the differing goals, structures, and approval processes of the First Nations and government negotiators. Municipalities don t have a seat at the negotiating table and may have limited The lengthy timelines add to the uncertainty for municipalities for example, Whitehorse was not able to develop the waterfront land because they knew that the land was a key issue in the negotiations with the Kwanlin D n. Municipalities may be concerned about the loss of property tax revenue for land included in agreements with First Nations, implications for servicing of the land, and the ability to move through the First Nations land to access other parts of the municipality. Bringing it Together What can we learn from this brief historical overview of the relationship between municipalities and Indigenous peoples? Pause and Reflect Take a few minutes to reflect on the material presented. You may note some similarities between our study of local government and this module s overview of Indigenous governance. What are they? Are there also important differences? What do these similarities and differences mean for our studies of local government and Indigenous relationships? There are some similarities in governance structure and responsibilities. Both municipalities and First Nations administer a specific, defined jurisdiction; both provide services, develop policies within their jurisdiction, and pass bylaws. It has been estimated that about 80 of the day-to-day concerns of municipal councils would be the same as those of First Nations councils (Tennant as referenced by McAllister, 2004, 24). Both band councils and municipalities are defined in legislation and both have limited autonomy, with the potential for a decision to be overridden by the province or federal minister. Both have limited powers of taxation and revenue tools; both are governed by an elected council and leader. : Similarities While First Nations and municipalities may be comparable, First Nations reject the characterization of their government as municipal (Alcantara and Nelles, 2009, 710). There are some key differences between municipalities and First Nations. First Nations have a constitutional relationship with the federal government and provinces, while provinces establish municipalities, which have no constitutional status. First Nations that have negotiated self-governance have a very different relationship with the federal and provincial government based on the agreement. If a First Nation has negotiated self-governance, it is able to raise funds through property and sales tax (Poholka, 2016, 29). Municipalities have the ability to apply special taxes hotel, billboards, etc. but they can t establish a sales tax. While some governance features are similar, First Nations have different governance traditions (Bish and Cassidy as referenced in McAllister, 2004, 24), which include both hereditary and elected band council governance. First Nations governance emphasizes collective rights that are held by the community rather th
Apr 06 08:15:08 raspberrypi node[7671]: an individual rights (Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing, 2009). There is more community engagement and participation, chiefs have less power than mayors, and decision-making is consensus focused rather than the majority-rule of municipal councils . In addition, elders play a key role in governance. Different Governance Processes and Traditions The Iroquois Confederacy uses Kaianerekowa, the Great Law of Peace, to guide their decision-making process. Wampum 5 emphasizes participation in the decision-making process, deliberation, diverse perspectives and respect for those perspectives, and consensus on the decision. The Kahmawa:ke First Nations, located south of Montreal, creates three groups of community members. Two of the groups discuss the issue and possibly amend the options under consideration. A third group watches the back and forth between the two groups and gives feedback at the end of the discussion. All three groups must agree on the decision, otherwise the proposal doesn t move forward in the process for a council decision. In Peace, Power, Righteousness: An Indigenous Manifesto, Gerald Taiaiake Alfred reflects Our traditions demand a higher standard of conduct in fact, a completely different conception of the leader s role than do the conventional corporate models that dominate business and policies in mainstream society. Simply put, for us it is not enough to know how to : Differences gain, hold and use power. Like my forebears, I believe that leadership consists in invoking the power of reason and that the human capacity to achieve harmony is best developed through pacification and persuasion. (as quoted by Meslin, 2019, 203). Interested in learning more? Here are two resources: The establishment of the Kaianerekowa (great law) Kayanerehkowa, the great law of peace It is also important to recognize that there are different local government relationships for Indigenous peoples living on reserve and those living off-reserve. People living off-reserve do not have a unique system of governance or representation they are part of the municipality. First Nations Governance The earlier discussion showed that Indigenous governance is both complicated and evolving; it is fair to say that the relationship that municipalities have with First Nations governments is also complicated and evolving. Before we consider the types of relationships and look at some examples, let s review the forms of First Nations governments. The Government of Canada has recognized 6 First Nations (OECD, 2019, Key Debates). These First Nations can have different governance structures under different pieces of legislation or agreement. Indian Act governance This is the form of government imposed under the Indian Act, which requires elections of a band council and chief every two years. As noted earlier, two recent pieces of legislation have provided opportunities for First Nations to assume more responsibility and autonomy. The First Nations Land Management Act delegated land management responsibilities from the Indian Act to band councils, and the First Nations Fiscal Management Act 2006 gave First Nations jurisdiction over core government functions. Self-governance The governance of Indigenous communities is changing as First Nations negotiate treaties and self-governance agreements with the federal government. Self-governance can take different forms it can be developed based on the unique characteristics of the Indigenous community or it can take a more public form. Traditional Indigenous governance combines hereditary traditional governance, including elders and or representatives from clans, with some elected positions. The structure of committees and the decision-making process will vary among First Nations. Public governance is when the governance process, including elections, is open to all residents of the community territory. Working Together Municipal First Nations Alcantara and Nelles collected and classified 332 formal municipal First Nations agreements from 1950 to 2014. These agreements varied some were short-term and transactional, while others were longer-term and relationship focused. Alcantara and Nelles identified four types of agreements (Nelles and Alcantara, 2011; Alcantara and Nelles, 2016): 1. Relationship-building agreements emphasize respect, mutual recognition, transparency, and communication. They generally include a commitment to collaborate or cooperate. 2. Decolonization agreements recognize that a municipality is using land that was historically occupied by the First Nation and acknowledge the rights and interests of the First Nation to their traditional land. They generally include an intention to develop a longer-term relationship and principles to guide the development of the relationship. 3. Capacity-building agreements focus on municipal support for the development of First Nations governance or institutional capacity. They are one-way relationships and are quite rare. 4. Jurisdictional negotiation agreements can take two forms they can relate to service provision for a fee by one party for the other, or to the more collaborative joint management of a resource, service, or structure. They include shared service agreements, contracted services, legal contracts, or land leases. The earliest formal agreements between municipalities and First Nations, beginning in the 1950s, related to joint service provision. The number of formal agreements increased significantly since the 1990s, and more than two-thirds of the agreements were recorded between 2000 and 2014 (Alcantara and Nelles, 2016, 26). In particular, the number of relationship-building and jurisdictional negotiation agreements, both the service-related agreements and joint management agreements, increased since the 1990s. This signals a shift in relations between First Nations and proximate local governments towards a more cooperative, collaborative, and perhaps decolonized inter-governmental relationship based on principles of mutual respect and interest (Nelles and Alcantara, 2011, 326). In addition to the variation over time, there is variation between provinces. The number and type of agreements vary significantly by province, with British Columbia and Ontario reporting the most formal agreements in the 64-year period (Alcantara and Nelles, 2016, 26). Two factors have an influence on the decision to engage in a formal municipal First Nations agreement: capacity and having the tools and resources to participate in a relationship, and willingness to use the capacity in developing a formal relationship (Alcantara and Nelles, 2016, 36). It is important to note that municipal-Indigenous relationships are also developed through municipal associations. The Federation of Canadian Municipalities has created a number of resources, guides, as well as joint funding programs and other initiatives to support the development and maintenance of strong relationships. Similar initiatives are underway at the provincial level. The Union of British Columbia Municipalities held a First Nations Summit in collaboration with their Aboriginal counterparts that resulted in a protocol to share information and build relationships and to jointly administer a Community to Community Forum Program. You are encouraged to look at the FCM and your provincial municipal association to explore the range of initiatives. The previous discussion looked at the type of formal agreements between municipalities and First Nations. This section shifts the focus to the nature of the overall relationship, recognizing that there may be multiple and different types of agreements that contribute to the overall relationship between the two parties. Nations relationships. The video First Nations-Municipal Collaboration describes some of those partnerships. Alcantara and Nelles proposed that relationships could be classified, based on the level of engagement of the parties and the level of intensity of the relationship (Nelles and Alcantara, 2011; Alcantara and Nelles, 2016). Their relationship matrix identified four relationship types, which are described below. type. High Engagement Level High Intensity Strong synergy An institutionalized partnership with ongoing formal and informal contacts, such as the joint management of a facility or resource. The Village of Teslin (the Village) and Teslin Tlingit Council (the Council) are located in the Yukon. Teslin Tlingit was one of the first First Nations to negotiate self-government agreements. It includes representatives from the five clans on the Tesling Tlingit Council, and follows an : Village of Teslin and Teslin Tlingit Council Aboriginal self-governance model (Alcantara and Nelles, 2016, 71). The Council and the Village signed five agreements between 2005 and 2015 based on their history of collaboration and a positive and friendly relationship between the two communities: An accord that recognized the importance of mutually beneficial relationships. It included maintenance of monthly meetings and an agreement to cooperate in the future. The agreement encouraged both partners to consider forming a regional administration and planning structure and to cooperate on quality services at cost effective prices. Construction of new sewer line through the Council lands, joint involvement in design and management of construction, with future right for the Council to connect to the pipe. The Council built a skateboard park in the Village, near an existing arena, with a financial contribution from the Village, and a commitment to shared maintenance and management of the facility. Development of an integrated community sustainability plan for the whole community (the Village and the Council) including shared vision, values, and goals. Recreation contribution agreement for the joint management of recreation programs for both communities. Low Intensity In the loop The relationship involves sharing information and connections between the partners; it may or may not lead to a more formal relationship. The Village of Haines Junction (the Village), the Champagne First Nation, and the Aishihik First Nation are located in the Yukon Territory. They have entered into four service agreements and three relationship-building agreements: Animal control service agreement signed in 1 Water and sewer services Fire protection agreement Solid waste removal and disposal Agreement to meet quarterly Agreement to meet to coordinate economic development activities : Village of Haines Junction and Champagne and Aishihik First Nations Low Engagement Level Agreement to meet annually to discuss shared issues While these three communities developed strong and engaged relationships, they haven t led to more intense joint management or joint governance process relationships. High Intensity Agreement-centred The relationship is defined through the agreement there is no relationship other than that defined in the agreement. The Regional Municipality of Les Basques and the Mal cite de Viger First Nation are located in eastern Quebec. The municipality and First Nation entered an agreement to jointly establish and manage the Inter-Nations Regional Park through a new nonprofit organization. The agreement was signed in 2014 to manage and maintain the 256 square kilometer park for public use. There had been little interaction between the municipality and the First Nation prior to the agreement. Despite this, they both had a strong interest in collaborating to create the park and the result was described as both intense and unique (Alcantara and Nelles, 2016, 133). Low Intensity Business as usual These can be described as business transactions rather than ongoing relationships. They could include agreements related to provision of services for a fee. Sault Ste. The emergence of these partnerships reflects a growing recognition among Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal actors across Canada that cooperation, coordination and communication at the local level are necessary for dealing with a host of practical problems that affect both communities, jointly and separately (Nelles and Alcantara, 2011, 330). Urban Reserves Municipalities also engage with First Nations with respect to urban reserves. These are pieces of land within or adjacent to municipalities that are owned by First Nations and classified with reserve status by the federal government. The land may have been part of a land claim agreement settlement with the Government of Canada, or may have been purchased with funds transferred as a result of a land claim agreement, or earned by a First Nation. The reserves can be additions to existing First Nations reserves or new reserves for a First Nation that didn t previously have designated territory. In 2013, it was estimated that there were about 120 urban reserves in Canada, mostly in Manitoba and Saskatchewan (Poholka, 2016, 6). Urban reserves are not easy to establish there is a lengthy, multi- year process for the land to be declared as a reserve by the Government of Canada that involves consultation with the municipality, the community, and province. 911 service agreement signed in 1996 10-year lease of land from Garden River to Sault Ste. Marie so that the city can build an ambulance station. The ambulance station is a city facility staffed with First Nations band members. Sault Ste. Marie has nine agreements with Batchewana First Nation: Four agreements involved the provision of fire protection (agreements signed in 1991, 1999, 2004, and 2008) Sewage treatment Provision of water services 911 service calls Shared winter maintenance of two streets adjacent to both communities Road extension related to future development in both communities Most of these agreements involve the provision of services by one partner to the other for a fee. Urban reserves provide First Nations with opportunities to generate revenues and may provide a place where they can offer services to band members living in the municipality. They provide municipalities with the opportunity to develop stronger and more meaningful relationships with First Nations and to benefit from the economic development activities on the urban reserve. However, they can also lead to tensions, and municipalities may be concerned about the loss of municipal revenues, unfair competition from businesses located on the urban reserve, as well as potential planning and bylaw issues. There is uneven understanding of urban reserves that may contribute to those perceptions research found that municipalities had a limited understanding of some of the policies and processes related to urban reserves (Poholka, 2016, 35). Did You Know? In an effort to promote better understanding of urban reserves and the value of strong relationships with First Nations, the City of Saskatoon website includes information for residents and businesses about urban reserves and treaty land entitlement. There are profiles of each First Nation, a map of land holdings or reserves in Saskatoon, answers to frequently asked questions , as well as links to details about Indigenous initiatives. Provinces have prepared guidelines about urban reserves. Manitoba advises that the details about an urban reserve must be negotiated between the First Nation and municipality before the federal government gives approval of the urban reserve. The Municipal Development and Services Agreement (about the reserve) will include tax issues, harmonization of bylaws, issues of access, process for communication and planning, and a dispute resolution processes. Toolkits and templates are available through the Federation of Canadian Municipalities . Did You Know? Muskeg Lake Cree Nation The Muskeg Lake Cree Nation was the first urban reserve in Saskatoon, established in 1988 (see the link above for an introduction to the Muskeg Lake Cree Nation). The process to designate the land as an urban reserve took four years as described in the video Muskeg Lake Cree Nation Urban Reserve: A Journey Together (). Since then, there have been additions to the reserve lands and the urban reserve now includes 48 acres in Saskatoon. The city provides some municipal services for a fee, and the agreement includes provisions related to property tax losses and land use and establishes relationship protocols. Early in the process, the band council and Saskatoon city council held annual joint meetings, and communication is ongoing. The reserve provides employment for Indigenous and non-Indigenous people and generates property tax revenues for the Muskeg Lake Cree Nation. There were no issues with the land use the First Nation wanted the development to look and feel like other developments in the urban area.
