Reconciliation with Indigenous Peoples: A Holistic Approach Reconciliation in Practice A Holistic View A holistic view of reconciliation honours many Indigenous worldviews and can provide a useful framework for systemic change. A holistic approach considers four interconnected areas mental, physical, emotional and spiritual. This section offers some examples of how municipal initiatives designed to lead to reconciliation are progressing in each of these four areas. If we address each area in our reconciliation journey, we can begin to generate the systemic changes we aim to achieve. The graphic below shows one example of how municipalities can think about the four interconnected areas. In this graphic, Knowledge Systems are linked to the Mental Domain; Action Processes are linked to the Physical Domain; Belief Systems are linked to the Spiritual Domain; and Values and Protocols are linked to the Emotional Domain. Mental Spiritual Emotional Physical Knowledge Systems Action Processes Belief Systems Values and Protocols Toolkit for Inclusive Municipalities in Canada and Beyond Knowledge Systems Many municipalities are exploring the TRC Calls to Action and UNDRIP to consider how these might be implemented locally. Some municipalities have prepared for reconciliation by creating new policy, establishing new government departments, and creating new staff positions. An important part of the process is for municipalities to work jointly governments, communities, organizations and individuals to develop plans and strategies supporting reconciliation. Mental The City of Calgary, AB, is supported by the Calgary Aboriginal Urban Affairs Committee, which serves as an advisory committee to City Council. The Committee operates with a 10-Year Strategic Plan and reports annually to City Council on its achievements. Their work has resulted in three significant documents to advance reconciliation in partnership with the Kainai Nation, Siksika Nation, Wesley Nation, Chiniki Nation, Bearspaw Nation, Tsuut ina Nation, and Piikani Nation. The White Goose Flying Report is the City s response to the TRC Calls to Action. The Indigenous Policy Framework and the Indigenous Policy documents describe the local First Nations history and landscape prior to treaty and the importance of these in the City s planning and decision-making processes. The City of Lethbridge, AB, and the Lethbridge Indigenous Sharing Network have created a Reconciliation Implementation Plan that was unanimously adopted by City Council. The plan was developed in partnership with the Kainai Nation and the Piikani Nation. The City Council in Vancouver, BC, designated Vancouver as a City of Reconciliation and began initiatives to begin healing and forging new relationships. A Framework for City of Reconciliation was adopted, focusing on cultural competency, strengthening relations, and effective decision-making at the corporate level (within the overall service provision). Council also adopted the City s response to 2 TRC Calls to Action, identifying 4 City initiatives under three themes: Healthy Communities and Wellness; Achieving Indigenous Human Rights and Recognition; and Advancing Awareness, Knowledge and Capacity. The City of Prince George, BC, has adopted a Reconciliation Framework which contains corporate strategies based on the UNDRIP, recommendations from the TRC, and the City s Commitment to the Coalition of Inclusive Municipalities. Reconciliation with Indigenous Peoples: A Holistic Approach Action Processes Reconciliation involves multiple partners working in a positive relationship, with a willingness to collaborate. Successful partnerships often lead to policy development, tangible actions and greater understanding of diverse values and protocols. Truth and Reconcilation Commission of Canada Conclusion Transformation of social structures will take time and involve many different approaches. Indigenous communities make up less than 5 of the population of Canada, yet their involvement in reconciliation efforts by municipalities is crucial. Building new relationships is the work that lies ahead. Reconciliation will require open hearts and open minds, and a willingness to look at the world in a way that is more alert to, and respectful of, Indigenous peoples, and their rights and interests. It means honouring treaties and other commitments; it means acknowledging past harms and making a commitment to healing; it means changing the way we interact and the way we think about each other. Communities will benefit from courage, forgiveness, leadership and dedication. How will your community embrace reconciliation? Toolkit for Inclusive Municipalities in Canada and Beyond32 1. The Toronto Star. What Is a Budget? A budget is an estimate of revenues and expenditures for a particular period, usually 12 months. But municipal budgets are more than that. Budgets are the most important policy document of all levels of government, including local government they set out governments priorities and intentions for the coming year(s). Municipal budgets are part of a planning and management process. They follow from a strategic vision or set of priorities and reflect the short-term goals established by the local council. They link to an accountability, performance, and reporting process on how resources are used and the associated results and outcomes achieved. Budgets are also a key financial management tool of government they identify proposed expenditures, and they allow for monitoring, accountability, and control of how money was spent and where. Budgets directly affect the tax rate and set out charges such as user fees. There are two types of municipal budgets the operating budget and the capital budget. An operating budget reflects the costs and revenues associated with the ongoing, regular operations of the municipal services, programs, administration, and governance processes. Operating budgets must be balanced with expenditures balanced by offsetting revenues because provincial legislation prohibits municipalities from having an operating budget deficit. The capital budget is for large cost items associated with the development of new municipal infrastructure and assets or the replacement of existing ones. These include buildings, roads, vehicles, flood control infrastructure, and major computer systems. These items may be financed through loans, grants from other levels of government, or reserves that municipalities have accumulated over the years for those purposes. The costs of these items are typically amortized, or spread out over a number of years. Some municipalities also have rate supported programs like water or waste management that are separate from the operating and capital budget. The operational and capital needs of these programs are entirely funded by user charges or rates. budget. Most municipalities have a standard budget process that includes: Council-approved guidelines for staff regarding the upcoming budget Internal staff process to develop a draft budget Budget committee a committee of councillors who guide and review the development of the budget Council s final approval of the budget While this looks like a clear and tight process, the reality is anything but! Budget processes in large municipalities can take months, often starting in the fall and continuing into the following year. They are complex processes of estimating, forecasting, planning, balancing, and negotiating among many competing and compelling interests. Residents, community groups, civil society organizations, and businesses can have input on a municipal budget. Often municipalities hold special budget consultations, which provide information on the budget and offer opportunities for community members to ask questions and provide feedback. Community members can also make deputations to committees of council and or the budget committee and can send written feedback to their councillor or to one of the relevant committees. addition to written input. Here are two examples of these deputations: Business as Usual Is Not Enough, the speaking notes for a deputation from Jasmine Ramze Rezaee, Manager of Advocacy of the YWCA Toronto Toronto Budget Committee Deputation, January 2020 , a deputation from Sonya Yalda from the Toronto Youth Cabinet regarding funding for the TTC You are encouraged to look at the budget documentation for your local municipality. Most municipalities encourage public engagement and input, and budget material is often available in clear and plain language. Others have the treasurer s report, or a report from a budget committee, which sets out the various challenges and tradeoffs addressed in the budget. The City of Toronto, and other municipalities, make budget notes and other materials available to community members for service and program areas for example, here is one for Toronto Children s Services for 2020. Local social planning groups, boards of trade business associations, and residents associations are some of the groups that pay particular attention to municipal budget processes. You might also look at the websites of some these groups in your municipality to see their coverage and analysis of the most Other Approaches to Municipal Budgeting The typical approach to budgeting is one where the municipality, with opportunities for some public input, develops the budget, which then moves through the political approval process. Once approved, the budget is administered by staff. Many municipalities are opening up their budget processes to greater levels of engagement. Calgary has a process that includes surveys and questionnaires to rate city services, and then a vote on priorities. The city also has an app to inform residents about the budget and budget process and to support online discussion. Some municipalities are going further and trying a different approach to budgeting that features greater engagement in determining the municipal priorities and shaping how the money is spent. Participatory budgeting is different from regular budgeting because it gives community members the power to shape priorities and decide how some of the money is used. Participatory budgeting was first used in Porto Alegre, Brazil in the late 1980s. This city faced many challenges, including poor infrastructure, poverty, corruption, and limited engagement in local issues. Porto Alegre introduced a process where residents worked together to identify local needs and agree on the priorities, which then became part of the municipal budget. As a result of the process, municipal spending priorities changed, engagement increased, and corruption was reduced because there was greater awareness and accountability for how the money would be used. In addition, a World Bank review found that Porto Alegre had a 20 increase in sewer and water connections and a quadrupling of schools; the UN-Habitat declared participatory budgeting a best practice (as reported in Flynn, 2016). Since the successful Porto Alegre experience, municipalities in Canada and the U.S. have introduced participatory budgeting. Toronto Community Housing, one of the first public sector organizations in Canada to use participatory budgeting in 2001, now allocates funds in both its capital and operating budget for residents to administer. Since 2005, the City of Guelph grants an amount from the municipal budget to a local organization in support of a resident-led process to determine how the money will be spent. A City of Toronto pilot project in three wards between 2015 and 2017 demonstrated interest in greater levels of engagement in local budgeting and improvements but found that the process required high levels of support and resulted in frustration among residents when there weren t enough resources to meet all the community needs (City of Toronto, 2019). There are three main sources of revenue for operating budgets of municipalities in Canada: Property taxes accounted for an average of 48 of municipal revenues in Canada in 2016 (Johal, 2019, 4). In comparison, property taxes represented 32 of operating revenues in the City of : Property taxes Toronto in 2018 (City of Toronto, 2019, 39). Transfers, grants, and subsidies accounted for an average of 19 of municipal revenues in Canada in 2016 (Johal, 2019, 4). In comparison, transfers and grants represented 18 of operating revenues in the City of Toronto in 2018 . Other municipal revenues, including user fees, account for an average of 30 of municipal revenues in Canada in 2016 (a final 3 came from interest and transfers) (Johal, 2019, 4). In comparison, user fees represented 28 of operating revenues; other revenues, including other taxes, fines, permits, and fees were a further 13 in Toronto in 2018 . Municipalities can t just decide to impose a new tax or fee if they need more money. They must receive permission, through provincial legislation, to introduce the tax or fee. The table below shows the sources of municipal revenue, including property taxes and other own source revenues that are permitted in each province. It is important to note that municipalities currently use many but not all of them. For example, Toronto does not have a vehicle registration tax it was introduced in 2008 and eliminated in 2011 although the city has the authority to reintroduce one in the future without provincial permission. Municipal revenues can be fixed, where municipalities have little or no control of the revenue, such as grants or transfers from another level of government. Revenues can be variable, such as user fees, property taxes, and licenses, where the level of revenue varies based on the environment, the economic climate, or locally determined policy. Assessing Revenue Services What Is a Good Source of Revenue? Good sources of revenue are equitable, efficient, reliable, stable, and predictable. We need to ask the following questions: Is the revenue source fair and equitable? Equity can be assessed two ways: we can consider horizontal equity, whether people or households with similar income levels or situations are treated the same way, and vertical equity, where we assess whether all people or households are treated the same way and the impact of the revenue tool is equitable across the full population. Is the revenue source efficient? Is the revenue source internally efficient to delivery and administer, i.e., it doesn t cost more to administer than the revenue it generates. Is the revenue source externally efficient, with no negative impact on the economy or the community, i.e., it doesn t result in shifts in spending or activity that have negative implications for the community or for the anticipated revenue. : How do we assess the different revenue sources? Is the revenue source matched to the spending? The benefit principle stresses the importance of linking the type of revenue source to the type of spending (Kitchen and Slack, 206). Is the revenue source reliable, stable, and predictable? Is the revenue source visible, transparent, and accountable to the people who pay the tax? Let s look at two recent new taxes introduced in the City of Toronto to assess whether they are good Land Transfer Tax The municipal land transfer tax was introduced in 2008 in Toronto. It applies to buyers of property in Toronto and is calculated on a five-point sliding scale, based on the sale value of the property. In 2018, the tax brought in 730 million (a reduction from the 805 the previous year) or 5.3 of the 2018 operating budget (City of Toronto, 2019, 40). The tax is in addition to a pre-existing provincial land transfer tax. The answer is: not really. The tax on the transfer of land, based on a home sale, has no relationship to the benefits received from the tax the purchaser does not receive services because the revenues go into the general municipal revenues. The tax applies only to those purchasing property; those who remain in their homes or who rent don t pay the tax. The tax is not stable there is no way of predicting the number of homes that will be sold or the tax revenues associated with the sale values of the properties. In addition, the land transfer tax may introduce an incentive for homeowners not to move, which would have implications for the economy, impacting real estate agents, lawyers, movers, home renovators, etc. It is somewhat progressive with five rates of taxation based on a property s market value. Vehicle Registration Tax The 60 year vehicle registration tax was introduced by the City of Toronto in 2008. The goal was ultimately to direct the funds to car-related city services . It was estimated that the tax, which was to be phased in, would bring in 50 60 million per year. The tax was eliminated in 2011. The vehicle registration tax was fairly predictable and stable. The tax connected with driving a car and use of municipal transportation infrastructure and was intended to be used to support car- related services. At 60, it would not have an impact on vehicle ownership and it was priced at half : Is the land transfer tax a good revenue source? : Was the vehicle registration tax a good tax? the pre-existing provincial vehicle registration fee. The tax may have increased the incentive for car owners to use transit, but the tax wasn t onerous and any incentive would be limited. The vehicle registration tax was a flat fee that didn t take income into account, although it may have had a greater impact on wealthier households with more than one car. It was easy to collect. Before we look deeper at the three main sources of municipal revenue, let s review two terms that are used frequently in tax policy discussions. 1. Progressive taxation is when the rate of taxation rises with the ability to pay (usually income) a higher income person would pay a higher tax rate than the rate levied on a lower income person. 2. Regressive taxation is when the rate of taxation or the amount of tax remains constant regardless of the ability to pay, with the result that a higher income person will pay a lower portion of their income in tax than a lower income person. As you move through the discussion of the three revenue sources, consider whether they are progressive or regressive. Property Tax From their early beginnings to the present day, municipalities have raised most of their revenue through the property tax. The property tax is a tax on real estate, including land and building structures. Originally, funds raised from property taxes were used to pay for local property-related services, such as roads, fire services, and municipal infrastructure. However, over time, as municipalities assumed greater responsibilities, the taxes are now used to support property- and non-property-related services. Property taxes vary depending on whether the property is residential, commercial, industrial, or agricultural. Did You Know? Canada is an outlier among advanced economies in its reliance on property taxes to fund local governments. In 2017, local property tax revenues accounted for 3.2 percent of GDP in Canada, one of only two Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development member nations with a share above 3.0 percent (Johal, 2019, 5). Property taxes are paid by property owners, including those who own condominiums. Tenants also pay property taxes as part of their rent, but it isn t clearly distinguished and the bill doesn t go directly to them, with the result that they often don t know that they also contribute property taxes. The result is that home and condo owners are generally more interested in and knowledgeable about property tax and municipal issues and have a higher voter turnout in municipal elections than tenants. Property taxes are the largest source of own source revenue for local governments. Their importance in terms of total municipal revenues varies with the level of provincial support for municipalities. Largely, revenue from property taxes must make up the difference between provincial (and federal) grants and transfers and the cost of municipal services and programs. Some go so far as to suggest that the municipal tax rates reflect provincial policy and support for municipalities. How Are Property Taxes Calculated? Property taxes are based on the assessed value of property plus improvements. The responsibility for assessing the value of properties varies province to province. The Institute conducts original research on issues facing cities in Canada and around the world; promotes high-level discussion among Canada s government, academic, corporate, and community leaders through conferences and roundtables; and supports graduate and post- graduate students to build Canada s cadre of municipal finance and governance experts. Power and Purpose: in Transition Zack Taylor and Alec Dobson Abstract This overview of municipal law in Canada s 10 provinces identifies similarities and variations among and within provinces in the articulation of municipal purposes and the provincial-municipal relationship, municipal powers and jurisdiction, the organization of municipal institutions, and finance. The paper also comments on asymmetrical arrangements for large cities, commonly referred to as city charters. Far from being static, Canadian municipal law is in a period of transition. The legal scope of municipal authority has expanded over the past 25 years as most provinces have revised their general municipal acts and adopted special laws for major cities. While the overall trend has been toward more permissive authority and the recognition of municipalities as democratic, accountable, and responsible governments, there are significant variations across the provinces, and some have gone further than others in expanding the legal authority of municipalities. We conclude that the practical potential of this wave of legislative reform remains unknown and perhaps unrealized, and requires further research. intergovernmental relations JEL codes: H11, H Table of Contents About the Urban Project v About IMFG v Authors vi Acknowledgements vi Disclaimer vi Abstract 1 Power and Purpose: Canadian Municipal Law in Transition 5 1 Introduction 5 1 1 The provincial-municipal relationship: An enduring tension 5 1 2 What is municipal law? 8 1 3 Objectives, scope, and limitations 9 1 4 Outline of the paper 10 2. This is a constitutional fact, identical to American and Australian local governments relationship to their states, and British local authorities relationship to Parliament. In Anglo-American democracies, general-purpose municipalities are public corporations that derive their existence entirely from enactments of sovereign legislatures and exercise only the authority that is delegated to them by law. In the words of former Chief Justice McLachlin in Catalyst Paper Corp. v North Cowichan : Municipalities do not have direct powers under the Constitution. They possess only those powers that provincial legislatures delegate to them. This means that they must act within the legislative constraints the province has imposed on them. If they do not, their decisions or bylaws may be set aside on judicial review ( 1 SCR 5, at para. 11).1 Despite this narrow legal construction of local governments in Canada and elsewhere as corporations, municipalities are also understood to embody a second purpose: as accountable, democratic governing authorities representing localities. Local politicians and community leaders routinely demand greater legal autonomy and fiscal resources and condemn unilateral provincial actions in the local government sphere, arguing that the governments that are closest to local communities are the most sensitive to their needs and will make the best decisions for them. This tension between the central and the local has always been present, and always will be. Since before Confederation, the relationship between provincial and local government has shifted as public expectations of local government, and also the policy needs of an increasingly urban population, have changed. Three distinct trends are evident since the Second World War, and especially since the late 1990s. The first is local empowerment: provinces have generally expanded the scope of authority delegated to local governments, sometimes by adding specific areas of jurisdiction to municipalities express powers. A few have also 1. See also Greenbaum v Toronto, 1 S.C.R. 674, in which the Supreme Court of Canada declared: municipalities are entirely the creatures of provincial statutes. Accordingly, they can exercise only those powers which are explicitly conferred upon them by a provincial statute. See also Ontario Public School Boards Assn. v Ontario (Attorney General), , 1 DLR (4th) 346, in which the Ontario Supreme Court stated: Municipal governments and special purpose municipal institutions such as school boards are creatures of the provincial government. Subject to the constitutional limits in s. 93 of the Constitution Act, 1867, these institutions have no constitutional status or independent autonomy and the province has absolute and unfettered legal power to do with them as it wills. Zack Taylor and Alec Dobson - 6 - granted municipalities a broader, but still limited, general authority to accomplish locally determined ends and several have established separate legal or regulatory frameworks for large cities, sometimes known as city charters. Table 1.1 summarizes major changes to general municipal law and city charters. The chronology suggests that reform originated in Western Canada first before diffusing to Ontario, Quebec, and then to some of the Atlantic provinces. Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador are conspicuous for not following their peers. In addition, several provinces have restructured local government institutions including altering their boundaries to increase the municipal system s fiscal and administrative capacity to make and implement policies and deliver services. Provinces use legal mandates and conditional grants to direct or steer local priorities, particularly in housing, social policy, and land-use planning, either to provide a minimum level and consistent standard of service across the greater jurisdiction or to coordinate the policies of proximate local Zack Taylor and Alec Dobson - 8 - governments. At the same time, provinces make decisions that profoundly affect local government decision-making, including the financing, planning, and operation of large-scale infrastructure systems and facilities, such as highways and transit lines, trunk water and sewer systems, electricity production and distribution systems, and facilities such as hospitals and courthouses. On the face of it, local empowerment and provincial policy centralization embody contradictory impulses. Local governments have more authority and the capacity to exercise it than ever before, yet unilateral provincial government intervention in municipal affairs sometimes strategic, sometimes arbitrary continues. In certain domains, municipalities are policy takers, functioning as the field offices of provincial ministries; in others, they are policy makers, devising innovative solutions to local problems. Canadian governance is a web of federal, provincial, local, and Indigenous governments, agencies, and other public bodies whose authority, resources, and capacities are interwoven in complex ways. Provincial intervention and municipal autonomy inevitably coexist. Nevertheless, the question of whether the configuration of the provincial-municipal relationship reflects contemporary values and meets current needs is perennial. This paper informs this discussion by providing a comparative survey of the provincial statutory frameworks that govern municipalities. While we do not systematically review case law in this paper, the third trend is the expansion of judicial deference to local legislation. Since the 1990s, the Supreme Court of Canada has tended to interpret municipal action more generously, although it has not read a protected sphere of local self-governance into the constitution. 1.2 What is municipal law? Broadly construed, the body of municipal law includes all legislation, regulations, policy guidelines, and judicial and tribunal decisions that enable, constrain, and otherwise influence the activities of municipal corporations. Within this wide net, arriving at a precise number of provincial statutes that touch on the municipal domain is difficult. statutes that do so in Ontario, while the Association of Municipalities of Ontario estimates the number at 280. 2 And this does not include federal statutes on matters such as environmental and labour standards or public housing. A stricter definition includes only provincial statutes that establish the existence and primary authority of municipal corporations.3 This body of law is the focus of this paper. Box 1.1 highlights distinctions between general and special legislation in the municipal field. 2. Correspondence with the Association of Municipalities of Ontario, 8 October 2019. 3. The creation and empowerment of municipalities can occur through separate legal instruments. In Saskatchewan and British Columbia, a general statute empowers the executive to incorporate municipalities by order-in-council; however, the jurisdiction and authority of such municipalities is defined by the general act. Ontario and other provinces have used special laws to establish new municipalities (including through amalgamation), which draw their authority from a general Power and Purpose: Canadian Municipal Law in Transition - 9 - Box 1.1: General and Special Legislation: A Key Distinction Readers should note a technical distinction between two types of legislation general and special which is more commonly made in the United States than in Canada. Special legislation applies to a specific person or corporation General legislation, by contrast, applies to all subjects in the polity or a defined class (see Binney 1893). This distinction should not be confused with that between public and private legislation. The City of Toronto Act, 2006, and the Vancouver Incorporation Act, 1886, are special statutes because they each apply to one municipality only. Ontario s Municipal Act, 2001, is a unified general statute that applies to all municipalities except for the City of Toronto. Saskatchewan takes a less unified approach. It has separate general statutes for three categories of municipal corporations: cities, rural municipalities, and northern municipalities. the Cities and Towns Act applies to larger, urban ones. Both specify processes of incorporation and boundary change, as well as institutions and procedures. The grant of authority which defines municipal jurisdiction, however, is contained in a separate general Municipal Powers Act. 1.3 Objectives, scope, and limitations This paper examines the organization and scope of municipalities authority and responsibilities as defined in provincial laws to present an accessible, systematic, up-to-date comparison of provincial statutes that reveals commonality and variation across the country perhaps the first such comparison since Lidstone and Garcea . We do not systematically assess the degree to which municipalities make use of their authority. Indeed, municipalities may not fully exploit their legal authority. Such an assessment would require close examination of specific municipalities more than 3,000 in Canada and is beyond the scope of this paper. Rather, our goal is to describe the content of provincial legal frameworks for municipal government, focusing especially on comprehensive revisions to general municipal legislation made since the 1990s. Our coverage is necessarily selective. Of the many types of local public authorities in Canada school boards, watershed management boards, local improvement districts, and so on our focus is on general-purpose municipalities. Moreover, in keeping with the objectives of the Urban Project, our focus is on the enabling and constraining aspects of provincial legislation: what statute law directly empowers municipalities to do and what it prevents them from We do not discuss statutes ancillary to this focus, such as legislation governing the conduct of municipal elections, nor do we discuss municipalities regulatory authority over land use, private businesses, and building standards, provincially regulated pooled Zack Taylor and Alec Dobson - 10 - To catalogue these intricacies across the 10 provinces would be impracticable and obscure the broad patterns and trends we seek to identify. Finally, our focus is on statutory provisions, not case law, although we reference judicial interpretations of legislation from time to time. 1.4 Outline of the paper The remainder of the paper is divided into six sections: Section 2, Defining the Provincial-Municipal Relationship, discusses the recent adoption of statutory provisions that define or regulate the provincial-municipal relationship. In several provinces, statutes have been amended to recognize municipalities as a level or order of government or as democratic governments, to specify the purpose of local government, and to establish a provincial duty to consult municipalities before making decisions that affect them, including recognizing the role of municipal associations as interlocutors. Section 3, Powers and Jurisdiction, outlines the powers and areas of jurisdiction authorized in general municipal legislation Municipal Acts and equivalents that define the authority of all general-purpose local governments within each province or territory or of specific categories of municipalities. In Section 4, Institutions, we review statutory provisions governing institutional structures: municipal incorporation, internal organization, boundary changes, the organization of municipal councils, the authority to enter into formal relationships with other bodies, and municipal accountability. We focus on the differences in whether municipalities are empowered to create separate corporations, some of the options available to municipalities to provide services, the methods prescribed for the selection of municipal heads of council, the powers available to heads of council, the independent ability of municipalities to organize their own political structure, statutory measures respecting ethical standards and the accountability of municipal councillors, and legislative protections for municipal politicians. Section 5, Finance, catalogues the range of revenue sources authorized by provincial legislation for operating and capital purposes, including the scope of and Section 6, Asymmetrical Arrangements, describes several provinces use of special legislation and regulation to establish idiosyncratic powers, jurisdiction, and requirements for large cities, commonly referred to as city charters. In some cases, these charters have removed specific municipalities from the application of general municipal legislation so that the municipality s authority is derived from the special law; in others they take the form of special laws or regulations layered over the general framework. In the Conclusion we discuss variations in local government laws among provinces, identify trends, and draw conclusions for the future. Power and Purpose: Canadian Municipal Law in Transition - 11 - 2. A central task of provincial legal frameworks for local government is to define the relationship between a province and its municipalities. Yet for most of Canada s history, provinces did not articulate in their statutes an explicit purpose for local governments beyond specifying their specific functions, nor did they set out rules of engagement for provincial-municipal interactions. This absence makes more sense if we appreciate that in the British constitutional and legal tradition, municipal governments originated as corporations whose voting shareholders were local burghers or landowners and that until the 19th century, there was no legal distinction between public and private corporations. Only with the extension of the electoral franchise to the general adult population rather than property owners only (a process that in some Canadian provinces remained incomplete until well after the Second World War) did municipal councils become democratic, accountable, and representative bodies in any meaningful sense. Moreover, it was only in the postwar period, as the fiscal entanglements and principal-agent relationships between provinces and municipalities multiplied, that provincial-municipal interaction became understood as a form of intergovernmental relations parallel to, or nested within, Canadian federalism. At the same time, provincial-municipal relations increasingly involved the formalized interaction of provincial governments with municipal associations at an executive or political level . This context helps us understand why provinces have only recently added explicit articulations of municipalities purpose and democratic function, as well as a recognition of intergovernmental relationships, to general municipal laws (see Table 2.1).4 Each of these additions is discussed in turn. Some provinces emphasize providing good government and public services. Laws in Alberta, Saskatchewan (mirrored in the Cities Act and the Municipalities Act), Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island contain almost identical phrasing: The purposes of a municipality are (a) to provide good government; (b) to provide services, facilities or other things that, in the opinion of the council of the municipality, are necessary or desirable for all or a part of the municipality; and (c) to develop and maintain safe and viable communities. Some provinces include additional items. Saskatchewan and Prince Edward Island add providing for stewardship of the municipality s public assets. Alberta adds to foster the well-being of the environment, while Saskatchewan and New Brunswick include to foster economic, social and environmental well-being. Other provinces use wording that acknowledges municipalities as accountable and responsible democratic authorities, and even an order of government. The Nova Scotia Municipal Government Act states in its preamble that the Province recognizes that municipalities have legislative authority and responsibility with respect to the matters dealt with in this Act and that municipalities are a responsible order of government accountable to the people. Similarly, Ontario s Municipal Act states that Municipalities are created by the Province of Ontario to be responsible and accountable governments with respect to matters within their jurisdiction and each municipality is given powers and duties under this Act and many other Acts for the purpose of providing good government with respect to those matters. British Columbia s Community Charter goes perhaps the furthest in stating that Municipalities and their councils are recognized as an order of government within their jurisdiction that (a) is democratically elected, autonomous, responsible, and accountable, (b) is established and continued by the will of the residents of their communities, and (c) provides for the municipal purposes of their communities. Qu bec s Municipal Powers Act and Cities and Towns Act do not articulate a purpose for local government. However, the preamble to Qu bec s omnibus Bill 122, An Act Mainly to Recognize that Municipalities are Local Governments and to Increase Their Autonomy and Powers (2017, c. 13), states that the National Assembly recognizes that municipalities are, in the exercise of their powers, local governments that are an integral part of the Qu bec State and that elected municipal officers have the necessary legitimacy, from a representative democracy perspective, to govern according to their powers and responsibilities. 2.2 Duty to consult British Columbia and Ontario have also legislated a duty on the part of the province to consult municipalities, individually or collectively, before making decisions that affect them. Powers and Jurisdiction 3.1 Grant of authority All municipal legislation contains a grant of authority, that is, a set of provisions that delegate to municipalities particular roles and responsibilities. These can be more or less general in their construction, at one extreme enabling municipalities to perform only enumerated functions, at the other defining general fields within which municipalities have broad discretion. Grants of authority are both enabling and constraining, in that they not only create municipal authority, they also limit it to certain subjects and circumscribe its use. Broadly speaking, grants of authority have become more expansive since the 1990s, when the cycle of statutory modernization began with Alberta s revised This section discusses provisions found in general municipal legislation, that is, legislation applying to all municipalities or categories of municipalities. So-called big city charters are discussed in Section 6. 3.1.1 General welfare power A municipality s general welfare power typically refers to an omnibus provision in the provincial enabling statute giving municipalities power to act for their own well- being, and for the well-being of their residents. Provincial legislation uses a variety of phrases to describe the general welfare power of municipalities. Alberta s Municipal Government Act gives municipalities power to pass bylaws for the safety, health and welfare of people and the protection of people and property (s. 7). The Municipal Powers Act of Qu bec gives local municipalities the power to pass bylaws to ensure peace, order, good government, and the general welfare of its citizens (s. 85). The Ontario Municipal Act empowers municipalities to pass bylaws for the economic, social and environmental well-being of the municipality, and the health, safety and well-being of persons (s. 11). Elsewhere, the general welfare power arises by implication through an interrelationship between the statutory purposes of the municipality described in the empowering statute(s) and the powers afforded to the municipality to achieve its purposes. For example, in British Columbia, sections 3 and 4(1) of the Community Charter provide that: 3. The purposes of this Act are to provide municipalities and their councils with (b) the authority and discretion to address existing and future community needs, and (c) the flexibility to determine the public interest of their communities and to respond to different needs and changing circumstances of their communities; and 4 (1). The powers conferred on municipalities and their councils under this Act or the Local Government Act must be interpreted broadly in accordance with the purposes of those Acts and in accordance with municipal purposes. Newfoundland and Labrador is the only province that does not grant its municipalities an omnibus general welfare power. While the province has held Zack Taylor and Alec Dobson - 16 - consultations on modernizing its municipal laws , it has not yet done so. 3.1.2 Express powers Before the 1990s, and dating back to the colonial period, most municipal legislation restrictively defined municipalities jurisdiction by enumerating lists of discrete powers (Lidstone 2007, 402 403). Municipalities were authorized to perform only those functions that were expressly included hence its characterization as the express powers doctrine. This approach was reinforced by the Canadian courts prior to the 1990s, which Makuch, Craik, and Meisk describe as follows: The courts, as a result of this inferior legal position, have traditionally interpreted narrowly statutes respecting grants of powers to municipalities. This approach may be described as Dillon s Rule, which states that a municipality may exercise only those powers expressly conferred by statute, those powers necessarily or fairly implied by the express power in the statute, and those indispensable powers essential and not merely convenient to the effectuation of the purposes of the corporation. Listing express powers has the advantage of affording municipalities certainty that bylaws and regulations passed in conformity with the enumerated powers will not be found to be ultra vires that is, beyond municipal jurisdiction. Yet no list of express powers can be exhaustive. In Canada, as in the United States, the need to adapt to changing circumstances has led municipalities to petition the legislature for amendments to general legislation or for special legislation to permit additional functions. The consequent burden on legislative committees spurred the creation of municipal boards and departments and ministries of municipal affairs in the early 20th century (Taylor 2019, 57 59). This legislative scheme is now used in the municipal statutes of eight provinces, with considerable provincial variation, and in some separate city statutes, including those for Winnipeg (a hybrid form), Toronto, and Montr al. Nevertheless, as Table 3.1 shows, all provincial statutes retain some express powers that apply to specific municipal needs. The number and specificity of spheres has increased over time. While Alberta s 1994 statute the first to establish spheres of jurisdiction (LeSage and McMillan 2008, 16) contains nine, more recent municipal legislation contains even more. New Brunswick s Local Governance Act, which came into effect in 2018, has 18 spheres, and Prince Edward Island s 2 Municipal Government Act specifies 21 spheres. General municipal laws in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador do not provide for spheres of jurisdiction. For a summary of the spheres identified in each province s legislation, see Table 3.2. In British Columbia, the Community Charter distinguishes between spheres exclusive to municipal governments and spheres shared by the province and municipalities, which require provincial sanction (s. 9). The British Columbia Court of Appeal has commented on the impact of the concurrent spheres in the Canadian Plastic Bag Association case, in which the Court of Appeal quashed a Victoria city council bylaw made without provincial approval. (As of this writing, Victoria is seeking leave to appeal the decision to the Supreme Court of Canada.) Further, in British Columbia, neither the Local Government Act (which governs the powers available to regional districts and electoral areas) nor the Vancouver Charter describe spheres of powers; instead, these two statutes rely on the enumeration of detailed express powers. In Ontario, the Municipal Act, 2001, sets forth 11 broad permissive powers, or spheres of jurisdiction (s. 11(3)), which can be exercised by lower-tier or upper- tier municipalities, as well as rules prescribing the division of authority in two- tier systems (s. 11(4)). In addition, the Act sets out eight matters under which municipalities can pass bylaws (s. 11(2)). Lidstone argues that the broad interpretation of the municipal general welfare power began to gain acceptance at the time of the Supreme Court of Canada s decision in the Shell Canada Products case. In that decision, the dissent, written by Justice McLachlin, urged that courts adopt a generous, deferential standard of review toward the decisions of municipalities in part because a generous approach to municipal powers is arguably more in keeping with the true nature of modern municipalities (Lidstone 2007, 405 406). Following the Shell Canada Products decision, the Supreme Court of Canada has tended to adopt the reasoning of the minority in that case, and has given impugned Zack Taylor and Alec Dobson - 20 - municipal bylaws a broad and deferential interpretation in the Rascal Trucking, Spraytech, and United Taxi Drivers decisions (see Makuch and Schuman 2015, s. 1). Nevertheless, the provinces retain constitutional authority over municipalities within the fields of provincial jurisdiction, as shown in the 2019 decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal in the Toronto city wards case (Toronto v Ontario). (As of this writing, Toronto is seeking leave to appeal this decision to the Supreme Court of Canada.) 3.2 Natural person power Natural person power enables a corporation to act as an individual in areas such as entering contracts, suing or being sued, hiring and firing employees, and taking any other corporate acts not prohibited by law. During the 1970s, most provinces modernized their corporation laws to give business corporations expansive powers akin to those of a human being in legal terms, a natural person (St. Paul ). In recognition of municipalities legal status as corporations empowered to exercise powers on behalf of their electors and residents, some provincial governments extended natural person power to municipalities to mimic the powers of provincially mandated business corporations. The grant of natural person power does not create new enumerated powers or spheres of jurisdiction, but potentially expands the municipality s ability to act independently within its areas of jurisdiction as established in provincial law. 3.2.1 Uneven extension and lim

While the pace of change has been uneven across the country, the trend has been toward greater empowerment and permissive application. Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and Labrador are conspicuous in having neither established spheres of jurisdiction nor conferred natural person powers. 3. The courts have increasingly demonstrated a generous interpretation of municipal authority. The courts have not only tested the limits of local authority, but also expanded the legal meaning of grants of authority. While sustaining the constitutional construction of municipalities as creatures of the provinces, the judicial interpretation of local bylaws has become more generous and deferential since the dissent by Justice McLachlin in the Supreme Court of Canada s 1 Shell decision, in which she stated that Courts should not be quick to substitute their views for those of elected council members on what will best serve the welfare of the city s citizens. The current and potential effect of more expansive judicial interpretation is not fully known, but, as we note later, worthy of systematic study. 4. Big cities increasingly operate under bespoke legal arrangements, but their long-term impact remains unclear. Much energy has been expended over the past 25 years on the idea of city charters, or what we characterize as asymmetrical arrangements for large cities. While the legal instruments differ, Toronto, Halifax, Calgary, and Edmonton have joined Vancouver, Winnipeg, Montr al, and other urban municipalities in deriving some or all of their authority from separate statutes relative to other cities. The constitutional relationship of municipalities to the province remains unchanged, however, and the powers available in special laws largely mirror those in general legislation. The modern wave of charter experimentation in Toronto and in the Alberta cities may represent a tentative first step toward greater asymmetry. Comfort with bespoke arrangements may lead to greater differences between charters and Alternatively, as seen in Ontario, general municipal law is often subsequently amended to incorporate the provisions in city charters. The adoption of charters may fuel a generalized thrust toward more expansive and permissive delegation of authority to municipalities in a ratchet effect. 5. Fiscal empowerment lags legal empowerment. The broad transformation in local government law we have described has not been accompanied by equally far- reaching changes in municipal access to own-source revenues. Few municipalities have access to revenues beyond property taxes, fees, and penalties for operating purposes, and borrowing for capital purposes. Most provinces also enable development charges and density bonusing to offset localized capital costs associated with development. Researchers have questioned whether the available revenue source mix is appropriate in a postindustrial economy and for large cities, and also whether municipalities have fully exploited their existing revenue sources. We have not discussed intergovernmental fiscal transfers because they are not a Two notable exceptions are the Federal Gas Tax Fund Power and Purpose: Canadian Municipal Law in Transition - 63 - block grant established in 2005 and Alberta s 2 City Charters Fiscal Framework Act, which establishes an ongoing statutory funding formula for Calgary and Edmonton. (The latter will be repealed and replaced with a less generous formula when Bill 20 comes fully into force.) Nevertheless, all local governments receive some combination of conditional and unconditional grants from the provincial governments by annual appropriation. The future will no doubt bring vigorous debate over whether and how much municipal fiscal stress should be addressed by: more intensive use of existing local revenue sources; enabling greater discretion in setting rates and how revenues can be spent (see, for example, Found 2019); increased unconditional support from the provincial and federal governments, perhaps through transferring a share of the federal GST; uploading responsibilities to provinces; or opening up new tax fields to municipalities, such as excise and payroll taxes. Regarding the last possibility, both theory and practice suggest that while revenue diversification is beneficial, strong political and competitive forces constrain any given municipality from imposing higher taxes than its neighbours (McMillan and Dahlby 2014; Tiebout 1956). Some have called for such taxes to be levied at the regional scale to minimize negative effects, and have noted significant variations in municipal tax bases: rich municipalities can raise more local revenue than poor ones. 7.2 Observations What have we learned from this review of municipal legislation? 1. We do not yet know the limits of existing municipal powers. The shift to more permissive grants of authority and the enactment of asymmetrical arrangements for large cities are recent. The full effect of these trends remains unknown and will be revealed only as local politicians and administrators devise initiatives that fully exploit their potential and statutes are interpreted by the courts. 2. While local self-government is a cornerstone of our political tradition, municipalities cannot be nation-states in miniature. Municipalities cannot go it alone because they are subject to larger economic, social, and environmental forces and are embedded in complex, historically evolved constitutional, legal, administrative, and fiscal systems. Municipalities need empowering legal and fiscal frameworks that reward creative problem-solving and democratic accountability without generating new inequalities and negative spillover effects. In establishing these frameworks, provinces must be constructive partners with municipalities. There is a risk, however, that greater municipal empowerment will reduce the incentive for provinces to maintain and support legal and fiscal frameworks much as home rule, both as a legal instrument and governing idea, has led American state governments to neglect the fiscal and other needs of their cities. Zack Taylor and Alec Dobson - 64 - 3. Insofar as provinces are engaged in local affairs, much depends on their wisdom and forbearance. Throughout this paper, we have emphasized the constitutional foundations of the provincial-municipal relationship. As constitutionally entrenched sovereign governments, provinces can alter laws, regulations, and policies affecting municipalities as they see fit. Whether they will do so wisely and strategically is a political question, not a legal one. 4. Greater institutional autonomy may be the next frontier. Compared with the United States, the internal organization of Canadian municipal representative and administrative institutions is highly uniform, because of prescriptive provincial legislation. It is an open question whether a more permissive legal approach for example, enabling municipalities to adopt strong mayors, partisan elections, or other variations would spur more innovative policymaking, more accountability and transparency, or greater operational efficiency. For example, Ontario s enabling of alternative electoral systems (see Municipal Elections Act, s. 41.1, which enables ranked-choice ballots) indicates the potential for municipalities to make such important institutional decisions on their own. 7.3 Suggestions for further research This paper has provided a general overview of provincial legal frameworks that constitute, empower, and constrain municipalities. The intricacies of general and special municipal laws and their legal interpretation in the 10 provinces require additional focused investigation. In particular, further research would be beneficial on three fronts: 1. This overview shows that municipal law is both enabling and constraining, and has become more permissive over time. What we do not fully understand, however, is exactly how constraints are experienced We recommend a survey of all Canadian municipalities, large and small and in all provinces, to identify what specific legal provisions (as opposed to fiscal limitations) prevent them from accomplishing important objectives. The results of such a survey would enable the focusing of reform advocacy on matters of everyday significance. 2. Case studies of municipal innovation using new legal tools. Municipalities have more powers than ever before, yet we know little about how they are being used. We recommend a research program to discover how municipalities are working at the limits of their legal authority to pursue policy objectives. In particular, we recommend focusing attention on bylaws and undertakings adopted on the basis of the general welfare power, broad grants of authority, and the natural person power. 3. Monitoring litigation and judicial interpretation. The meaning of statutes is fleshed out through legal challenges and judicial interpretations. We recommend the ongoing monitoring of court challenges to boundary-pushing municipal initiatives, as is performed by the FCM s Legal Defence Fund. Again, a key focus should be on Power and Purpose: Canadian Municipal Law in Transition - 65 - initiatives grounded in the general welfare power, the grant of authority, and the natural person power. This would not only reveal how the courts are interpreting the expanded powers and grants of authority in reformed municipal laws, it would also provide municipalities with insights on how to frame such bylaws. 8. 8.1 Documentary sources Althaus, Catherine, and Lindsay Tedds. 2016. TMU/Courses/2026/Winter/CFNF400 - Human Sexuality/Week 5 - Feb 7-13/Module/CFNF400, Module 5 - Learning Objectives.pdf","contentType":"application/pdf","size":534874,"folder":"week-5-cfnf400-module","listened":false,"lastChunkIndex":0,"totalChunks":18,"checkedChunks":null,"ttsAudioUrl":null,"ttsGeneratedAt":null,"extractedText":"By the end of this module, students will be able to: 1. Describe the attitudes of Canadians towards sexual orientation. 2. Recognize the major obstacles faced by gay, lesbian, and bisexual youth and adults. 3. Identify and describe the six stages of gay, lesbian, and bisexual identity development. 4. Identify and describe the four dimensions of the coming out process. Topic Overview In terms of the social context of human sexuality, the evolution of societal attitudes and public policies and laws related to sexual orientation represents a fundamental shift in basic assumptions about the very nature of human sexuality and in values concerning what is, and what is not, morally acceptable sexual behaviour. Sexual Orientation: Notes About Terminology and Acronyms Some terms related to sexuality can become, over time, politicized. Homosexuality is one of those terms. According to Cornelson \"The term 'homosexual' has a clinical connotation that is associated with pathology and reflects historical judgements that same-sex orientation was an illness. It is thus thought by many to be outdated, inaccurate, and even pejorative\" (). However, the term \"homosexuality\" is still used in the sexological literature (For example, your textbook uses this term but in a strictly non-pejorative sense.) Most people with same-sex attraction refer to themselves as \"gay\", \"lesbian\", or \"bisexual\", rather than as a \"homosexual.\" For the purposes of this course, the term \"homosexual\" is used in a value-neutral way that simply defines \"homosexuality\" as a sexual attraction to another person of the same gender. Various different acronyms have been used to describe the range of sexual orientations and gender identities that exist. Your textbook chapters on sexual orientation and gender define and discuss many of these identities. Here is an acronym currently used to define different sexually related identities. LGBTQI2SNA : Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, Two Spirit, nonbinary, asexual and other emerging identities . We will use the LGBTQI2SNA acronym at various points in the course. In Module 1 we contrasted the Restrictive and Permissive sexual ideologies. As we saw, according to Restrictive sexual ideology homosexual behaviour should be discouraged, whereas Permissive sexual ideology holds that sexual behaviours should be not be judged on the basis of the gender of the partners involved in a sexual act but rather on the basis of criteria such as whether the behaviour is consensual and mutually beneficial. On these grounds, Permissive sexual ideology holds that homosexual behaviours can have the same moral validity as heterosexual behaviours and that a person's sexual orientation is not in any way an indication of their psychological health. Increasingly, Canadian society is adopting a Permissive sexual ideology towards sexual orientation. Key Point Increasingly, Canadian society is adopting a Permissive sexual ideology towards sexual orientation. Below are the results of a surveys administered in 1975, 1995 96, 2006, and 2013 that measured adult Canadian's attitudes towards homosexuality (Bibby, 1995; 2006; Pew Research, 2014). Research on Canadians attitudes towards sexual orientation is revealing in a number of important ways: 1. The results reflect the trend, over time, towards a more permissive ideological perspective towards homosexuality among Canadians. For example, in 1975, 72 of adult Canadians believed that \"homosexual relations\" were \"Almost always wrong\" or \"Always wrong\". By 1995 96 the percentage of Canadians with this opinion had shrunk to 52 . In addition, the percentage of Canadians who felt that \"homosexual relations\" were \"Not wrong at all\" more than doubled from 14 in 1975 to 32 in 1995 96. When Bibby surveyed Canadians a third time a decade later he found that about two-thirds generally approved of homosexuality (Bibby, 2006, cited in Hyde, Delameter and Byers, 2009). In 2013, Pew Research asked Canadians: \"Do you believe that homosexuality is morally unacceptable, morally acceptable, or it is not a moral issue?\" Only 15 responded that is unacceptable while 30 said acceptable, 50 responded that it is not a moral issue, and 5 did not respond. 2. Although the data from these studies suggests that Canadians are becoming more accepting of homosexuality over time, the Canadian population remains segmented in its attitudes towards the moral acceptability of homosexual behaviour. Langstaff reviewed the evolution of Canadians attitudes towards homosexuality and found that although Canadian attitudes have become more accepting overall, much of the shift is the result of people who were more or less neutral about homosexuality shifting their views towards greater acceptance. From her analysis of the survey data, Langstaff concludes that people who have opposed homosexuality in the past have not changed their minds. Indeed, many of these people have become more firm in their dissaproval of homosexuality. According to Langstaff, although the percentage of Canadians who are accepting of homosexuality has increased, \"...a fairly stable minority of about one-third of Canadians are profoundly dismayed by growing societal acceptance of homosexuality\" (). However, as the Pew Research survey results, cited above, suggest, the percentage of Canadians who disapprove of gay, lesbian, and bisexual orientations is continuing to shrink. However, many people in Canada, are not fully accepting of diverse sexual orientations . attitudes-in-canada-toward-lgbt-individuals \"Whether or not one morally approves or disapproves of homosexual behaviour is immaterial to the principle inherent within a democratic society that all people, irrespective of their sexual orientation or other such characteristic, have the inalienable right to live a life free of discrimination\" . Key Point Over time, Canadian's attitudes towards diverse sexual orientations are becoming more accepting. While societal attitudes towards diverse sexual orientations are becoming more accepting, LGBTQI2SNA people live in a world where social and cultural conventions are overwhelmingly heterosexual and where their sexual orientation or gender identity is still often viewed with stigma and prejudice. Cultural representations in the media (e.g., advertising, entertainment) have, at least until very recently, been almost entirely heterosexual in nature. some religious institutions continue to disapprove of homosexuality. Sexuality education programs in the schools may be taught with the assumption that all the students in the class are heterosexual. Many gays, lesbians, and bisexuals have been the victims of violence that resulted from their being targeted because of their sexual orientation. Although all credible mental health professionals now consider homosexuality to be a normal variation of human sexuality, it should be noted that until quite recently, homosexuality was officially considered a mental illness or psychological disorder. For example, it was not until 1973 that the American Psychiatric Association removed homosexuality from its list of psychological disorders. It is in this heterosexually oriented social context that LGBTQI2SNA people form their personal identity as human beings. Key Point LGBTQI2SNA people grow up and achieve developmental tasks in a social environment where their sexuality or gender identity is often viewed with stigma and prejudice. Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual Developmental Tasks It is very important that we do not generalize about diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, treating them as if they were all the same. Each LGBTQI2SNA identity is unique. Here, we will focus specifically on the developmental tasks of people who identify as gay, lesbian, or bisexual. Being transgender refers to person's gender identity (e.g., woman, man, or non-binary: see Module 4). In Module 4, identity development among transgender people is discussed. It's also important that we recognize that a person's identity as gay, lesbian, bisexual, or transgender is just one component of identity and that it will overlap or intersect with other identities a person may have. An intersectional approach considers how different identities simultaneously affect an individual s experiences. An intersectional approach also recognizes that the discrimination and oppression that a person experiences based on sexual orientation may also intersect with other forms of oppression such as those based on race, class, sex, and gender identity. Challenges Facing Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual Youth As we proceed through this course we will be looking at the developmental tasks related to sexuality at the various phases of the life span (i.e., childhood, adolescence, adulthood, late adulthood). Gay, lesbian, and bisexual people must also face a series of challenges related to sexuality that heterosexual people do not face. This may particularly be the case for gay, lesbian, and bisexual adolescents who must navigate a heteronormative and often homophobic social world. These challenges are clearly apparent in a survey of youth's experiences of homophobia, biphobia, and transphobia in Canadian schools (Peter ., 2021: ). For example, according to the Peter . survey, 64 of students reported hearing homophobic comments at school and 30 of 2SLGBTQ students reported that they had been the victims of cyber bullying. For many gay, lesbian and bisexual people, their sexual orientation is a major defining characteristic of who they are as people. We will be looking at two fundamental aspects of personal and social development for gays, lesbians and bisexuals: stages of identity development and the dimensions of coming out. The term \"coming out\" is commonly thought of as the process of informing other people that one is gay, lesbian or bisexual. However, in reality, the process of coming out entails much more than simply telling other people about your sexual orientation. Key Point The coming out process involves much more than disclosure to others. According to Rosario, Hunter, Maguen, Gwadz and Smith the process of coming out involves four dimensions (see below). It is only with the fourth dimension that the person discloses to others that they are gay, lesbian, or bisexual. In a similar way, the individual's development of a gay, lesbian, or bisexual identity is not a single step process but rather involves a series of stages. Listed below are stages of gay, lesbian, and bisexual identity development and the dimensions of the coming out process. You will notice that in many ways the stages of identity development and the dimensions of the coming out process are parallel to each other. That is, for example, identity comparison, the second stage of identity development in which a person begins to understand that they are gay, lesbian, or bisexual and the first dimension of the coming out process, self-identification of sexual orientation are basically describing the same process: discovering feelings of same sex attraction. The important distinction we need to make is that the stages of identity development are focused on the person's internal psychological development whereas the dimensions of the coming out process are describing key factors of the person's social development as a gay, lesbian or bisexual person. For example, the stage of identity acceptance refers to the individual's acceptance in their own mind that they are in fact gay, lesbian or bisexual whereas, for example, the dimension of becoming involved in gay lesbian activities refers to the individual's social interaction with others. Together, the stages of identity development and the stages of coming out provide a basic conceptualization of the developmental tasks related to sexual orientation for gay, lesbian and bisexual people. It is also important to recognize that these processes of identity development and coming out occur within, and are a reflection of, the heteronormativity of our society. Heteronormativity is the assumption or belief that heterosexuality is the default, or \"normal\" form of sexual expression. It is within this heteronormative context that gay, lesbian, and bisexual people form their identity. As a result, we should not look upon these stages of identity development and dimensions of coming out as points along the road of ideal development but rather as points of struggle and progression that gay, lesbian, and bisexual people must face because of the heteronormativity of society. As heteronormativity fades as society progresses, these stages of identity development and dimensions of coming out will become less relevant. Key Point The stages of identity development relate to a person's internal psychological development. The dimensions of coming out relate to a person's social development. Both occur within, and are a reflection of, the heteronormativity of Western culture. Stages of Identity Development 1. Identity Confusion The person, usually in childhood, growing up in a heteronormative society, assumes they are heterosexual but has some feelings of same gender attraction. 2. Identity Comparison The person begins to recognize that they may be gay, lesbian, or bisexual. 3. Identity Tolerance The person more fully recognizes that that it is likely that they are in fact gay, lesbian or bisexual and may seek out contact with others in the gay, lesbian, and bisexual communities to find affirmation. 4. Identity Acceptance The person now fully recognizes that they are gay, lesbian, or bisexual and accepts their sexual orientation. 5. Identity Pride The person begins to accept their sexual orientation as a positive aspect of themselves and contrasts and differentiate themselves from heterosexuals. 6. Identity Synthesis The individual focuses on fully integrating their public and private identities as gay, lesbian, or bisexual. Dimensions of the Coming Out Process (Rosario, Hunter, Maguen, Gwadz and Smith, 2001) 1. Self-identification as gay, lesbian, or bisexual 2. Involvement in gay lesbian recreational and social activities 3. Attitudes towards GLB identities become more positive 4. Disclosure of sexual identity to others \"The coming out process is an individual experience. The milestones, the hurdles and the pace of the process, all vary from person to person. Individuals bring a variety of coping skills, problem- solving abilities and resources to the process\" . It is important to recognize that although the stages of identity development have been presented in a step by step linear fashion (i.e., in a 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 progression), many gay, lesbian, and bisexual people will not necessarily pass through all of these stages in the same order. For example, some individuals may not develop social links with the gay, lesbian, or bisexual communities until well after all the other stages have been completed. In terms of identity development, because they live in an often homophobic culture (see Chapter 9 of your textbook for a definition and discussion of homophobia), some gays, lesbians, and bisexuals struggle with the coming out process. Also, research shows that the timing and progression of the coming out process can be affected by intersectional factors such as gender, race, ethnicity, class, and generational factors (Grov, Bimbi, Nanin, and Parsons, 2006; Haltom and Ratcliff, 2021). 01776-x It is important to note that some people are quite critical of fixed stage models of gay, lesbian, and bisexual identity development. For example, Alderson believes that identity development is a highly individualized process that is affected by a wide range of factors. Not everyone goes through the same stages in the same order. However, acknowledging individual variations in processes and trajectories, stage models can be useful in understanding developmental processes of LGBTQ young people . A meta analysis of 30 studies indicated that common sequence of LGB identity development was becoming aware of queer attractions, questioning one's sexual orientation, self-identifying as LGB , coming out to others, engaging in sexual activity, and starting a romantic relationship . Key Point Not all individuals will progress through the stages of identity development in a step-by-step linear fashion. Although the stages of identity development and the dimensions of the coming out described above do not apply to everyone, they can be useful concepts for health professionals addressing the needs of gay, lesbian, and bisexual students and clients. For example, assessing the stage a person is at in terms of their identity and social development can be helpful in determining specific issues that need to be addressed and to determine if a client is making progress in their development. Discussing the stages with clients can help them to make a self-determination of where they are at and where they want to go next in terms of their personal development. There are a number of ways that the school system and educators can promote the health and well- being of LGBTQ students. These include developing school policies that create supportive environments, teacher and school staff training programs, developing and implementing LGBTQ inclusive school curricula, and fostering the development of LGBTQ student clubs, organizations, and alliances . Key Point Although they don't apply to everyone, the stages of identity development and the dimensions of the coming out process can be useful concepts for health professionals to consider in working with gay, lesbian, and bisexual clients. In the next five modules we will continue with the approach of using developmental tasks to examine sexuality in childhood, adolescence, adulthood, and late adulthood.
