Describe and evaluate societal attitudes towards adolescent sexuality and sexual behaviour. 2. Identify the key developmental tasks related to sexuality for adolescents. 3. Describe patterns of sexual behaviour during the adolescent years. 4. Identify and distinguish between the various influences on adolescent sexuality. Topic Overview Introduction: The biological and social context of adolescent sexuality It is perhaps stating the obvious to say that adolescence is a challenging part of our lives. One of the things that make it so challenging is that during adolescence nearly every aspect of our lives changes in profound ways. The physical, intellectual, emotional, and social domains of life are in state of rapid change beginning at puberty until we enter young adulthood in our early twenties. Of course, one of the areas where these changes are most prominent is sexuality. Sexual self-awareness may begin prior to adolescence and continues at an accelerated pace during adolescence and there is no doubt that, for most people, adolescence is a 'critical period' in the upsurge of sexual drives, the development of sexual values, and the initiation of sexual behaviours. The onset of puberty, the power of peer group expectations, and the communication of mixed messages about sex from adults can make dealing with sexuality difficult but for many, and hopefully most adolescents, the development of sexuality can be a positive and life enriching experience. Key Point Adolescence is a time of profound change in all aspects of life including sexuality. As we saw in Module Week 6, many of the building blocks of adult sexuality are built in childhood, but it is with the onset of puberty that we swiftly start to become sexual beings in the adult sense. In looking at the biological and social context of adolescent sexuality, it is important to note that beginning with puberty, youth are biologically capable of reproduction, have sexual feelings and desires, but, in Western society at least, they are about a decade away from assuming full adult status. We should keep in mind that until the twentieth century, in many respects, there was no such thing as adolescence. Soon after puberty, if not before, most people were out of school and often were married before their twentieth birthday. Obviously, this is not what happens for most Canadian youth today. According to sociologist Eleanor Maticka-Tyndale , What is new is the length of adolescence - that time between childhood and entry into roles are markers of adulthood (such as husband, wife, or parallel status; employee in a permanent job; rentee or mortgagee). Adolescence is a time when one is biologically mature but kept socially (and cognitively) immature, i.e., not ready to be an adult (). Furthermore, Lets be clear about this - these are social developments that are not tied to biology. Though young men and women enter puberty before they enter their teens, the average age of marriage is approaching 30. This means that by the time they marry young people have been biologically capable of reproduction for more than half their lives (Maticka-Tyndale, 2001, ). This gap between the biological readiness for sexual activity and the age at which we gain adult status has significant implications for how our society addresses adolescent sexuality. Although most teenagers are biologically ready to have sex, it is often said that teenagers are \"not mature enough\" to engage in sexual activity. Key Point In contemporary Western culture there is a significant gap between when young people become biologically capable of reproduction and the age at which most adults approve of young people having sex. The Developmental Tasks of Adolescent Sexuality For this course, we are looking at each phase of the life cycle in terms of specific developmental tasks related to sexuality. During adolescence, these developmental tasks are numerous and often difficult to accomplish. In one respect, the sexuality related developmental tasks of adolescence are confusing for the simple reason that adolescents live in a culture where they are biologically ready for sex, are constantly exposed to sexual imagery in the media, but at the same time they are often discouraged from expressing their sexuality by their parents, schools, and religious institutions. It is against the backdrop of this contradictory social context that we consider five major developmental tasks of adolescent sexuality. Key Point The developmental tasks of adolescent sexuality can be divided into five major categories: 1. Becoming comfortable with a rapidly changing body; 2. Gaining independence from parents family; 3. Developing self-acceptance as a sexual being; 4. Exploring romantic sexual relationships; 5. Protecting sexual health; 1. Becoming comfortable with a rapidly changing body: On average girls will begin puberty at age 10 or 11 and boys will begin at age 11 or 12. As anyone who has been through puberty knows, it is a time when both the mind and body are in a state of constant, often disconcerting change. (For an outline of the precise physical changes involved in puberty see Chapter 12 of your textbook). Physically, rapid increases in growth, development of secondary sex characteristics (e.g., pubic hair, facial hair, increased breast and genital growth), development of acne and body odour, menstruation, and other physical changes leaves many adolescents feeling awkward, insecure, and uncomfortable about their bodies. At one point or another, nearly all adolescents will wonder if their bodies are \"normal\" or will become convinced that they are unattractive. Media images depicting very narrow and unrealistic representations of the ideal body as well as peer group expectations can be very discouraging for adolescents struggling to gain confidence in themselves. On a general level, it is important for a person's overall well-being to become comfortable with their body. With respect to sexuality specifically, people who are comfortable with and accepting of their bodies are more likely to be comfortable and confident in their sexual relationships throughout their lives. 2. Gaining independence from parents family: Many theorists studying human development suggest that adolescence is a time when young people are seeking to establish a sense of their own identity as an individual. Put simply, adolescents are asking themselves \"Who am I?\" As part of the process of developing their own sense of self, adolescents will typically attempt to distance themselves from their parents and more closely align with their friends and peer group. Very often this move towards a sense of independence involves a rejection of parental values and norms including those related to sexuality. For example, some adolescents will reject their parent's wishes with respect to teen sexual behaviour, particularly if parental opinions conflict with teen peer group norms, as a way of asserting their independence and fulfilling a need to feel like an adult. Part of the general process of asking \"Who am I?\" is asking the question \"Who am I as a sexual person?\" 3. Developing Self-Acceptance as a Sexual Being: It's especially important that adolescents are able to integrate their sexual feelings, needs, and desires into a positive self identity, which includes, as one aspect, a sexual self. Put more simply, it is important for an adolescent to fully and consciously accept that they are a sexual being with sexual desires, needs, and feelings. We might assume, given the relatively open and permissive approach to sexuality in contemporary Western culture, that acceptance of the self as a sexual being is something that happens as a matter of course with all adolescents. However, some adolescents do have difficulty accepting themselves as sexual beings. This may particularly be the case for LGBTQI2S adolescents who have been exposed to homophobic attitudes. Fortunately, this is beginning to change as society becomes more accepting of diverse sexual identities, sexual minority youth navigate the developmental tasks of adolescent sexuality as well as their peers. Although Western culture has moved forward in recognizing and affirming female sexuality, to some extent, a sexual double standard between male and female adolescents still exists. In other words, our society is relatively more accepting of the sexual behaviour of teenage boys but looks more negatively upon teenage girls who are sexually active. Developing self-acceptance as a sexual being is important not only in terms of an adolescent's ability to form healthy current and future relationships. It is also important because people who do not acknowledge or accept themselves as sexual beings are less likely to take measures to protect their sexual health. For example, young people who do not acknowledge or accept themselves as sexual beings are less likely to plan to have sex or recognize that they might have sex. As a result, they are much less likely to practice safer sex if they do engage in sexual activity. This probably explains a significant proportion of unintended pregnancies and cases of STIs. 4. Exploring Romantic sexual Relationships: It is during adolescence that most young people will have their first romantic and or sexual relationship. Like most other aspects of teenage social life, romantic relationships typically cause a great deal of anxiety for adolescents. Many will have their first experience with falling in love and will be faced with the emotional turmoil of beginning and ending relationships. Adolescents are faced with the developmental task of learning, often with little or no experience, how to be in a mutually beneficial relationship and the experience they have with this process can have a significant influence on how they approach relationships throughout their lives. 5. Protecting Sexual Health: As you will see in your required reading for this module, the vast majority of Canadians become sexually active during adolescence and many teens are at high risk for HIV STIs and unintended pregnancy. Thus, learning the information and skills to consistently engage in behaviours that protect sexual health is a major developmental task of adolescent sexuality. Later we will explore how educational programs can effectively equip adolescents with the information, motivation, and behavioural skills to protect their sexual health. Patterns of Sexual Behaviour During the Adolescent Years Key Point The majority of Canadian young people will become sexually active by the time they reach age 20. The textbook documents various forms of sexual behaviour that occur in adolescence (i.e., masturbation, oral sex, intercourse). Approximately two thirds of Canadians will experience oral sex and or sexual intercourse before age 20. The most recent Statistics Canada data on sexual activity among young people indicates that the percentages of Canadian youth aged 15 to 24 who have experienced intercourse has not been increasing in recent years and may even be declining (Rotermann and McKay, 2020; SIECCAN, 2020). When reading about adolescent sexual behaviour, keep the following three Key Points in mind. Key Point Adolescent sexual behaviour is characterized by serial monogamy. 1) It is important to note that although most youth become sexually active at some point during adolescence, their sexual behaviour is often sporadic. That is, many, if not most, adolescents do not have sex on a regular or consistent basis. The literature on adolescent sexuality often designates a teenager who has had sex once as being \"sexually active\" even if that one time occurred several years in the past. However, it is not uncommon for a teenager, particularly a younger teen, to have sex only a few times over a number of years and to have a small number of sexual partners. Part of this is due to the fact that adolescent romantic sexual relationships are often relatively short in duration compared to adult relationships. Nevertheless, it is important to recognize that there is a subset of adolescents who are highly sexually active both in terms of frequency and number of sexual partners. Key Point Adolescent sexual behaviour is often sporadic and adolescent romantic sexual relationships tend to be relatively short in duration. 2) It is important to consider the concept of serial monogamy in order to understand patterns of sexual behaviour among adolescents and young adults. Most (but certainly not all) sexually active people are monogamous. That is, a person will only have one sexual partner at a time. Once a relationship ends, however, the person moves on to a new relationship where they again only have one sexual partner. Looked at in this way, a person could have four sexual partners in four successive relationships over a two-year period but still be monogamous. This person is more accurately described as serially monogamous. (See chapter 7 of your textbook for a discussion of \"friends with benefits\" relationships). The concept of serial monogamy is important to consider with respect to the high rates of STI among young people. For example, it is very common for college university students to be serially monogamous. Many college university students assume that they do not need to use condoms because they are in a monogamous relationship and neither partner shows any signs of having an STI (note that most cases of STI infection are asymptomatic so the person does not know that he or she is infected). These couples often use the contraceptive pill to prevent pregnancy but take no precautions against HIV STI. Psychologically, monogamous college university students often do not consider that they will very likely have different sexual partners in future monogamous relationships. In the end, by the time they graduate from university, many monogamous students will have had two, three, or more relationships, all of them monogamous, none of them protected from HIV STI. The occurrence of unprotected serial monogamy explains a large proportion of STI infections among college university students (For discussion of serial monogamy and its associated STI risk among college students see Bolton, McKay and Scnieder, 2010). Key Point Western culture provides youth with little education or guidance in developing the ability to have sexual relationships characterized by intimacy, mutuality, and pleasure. 3) The sexuality education provided to youth in Western culture, whether it is delivered by parents, schools, or other sources, is often limited to information on preventing sexual health problems such as HIV STD or is aimed at discouraging youth from becoming sexually active. As we have seen, most people will have their first sexual experiences during the adolescent years but many will do so lacking in accurate knowledge of human sexual response or the skills to have mutually pleasurable sexual relationships. As a result, these first sexual experiences can be a disappointment both physically and emotionally. Adolescents are generally left to trial and error as well as questionable advice from peers or distorted media representations for information on sexual intimacy and pleasure. Modern communication technologies (e.g., cell phones smartphones, social media apps websites) have fundamentally changed the way people are exposed to, learn about, and communicate with respect to sexuality. These technologies can have benefits (e.g., increased access to sexuality information, connecting with relationship partners), but also pose significant challenges (e.g., misinformation, privacy, and exploitation risks of online communication). Many people will be exposed to media portrayals of gender and sexuality (e.g., via social media, movies television music videos online games, pornography) that challenge sexual health and well-being in either positive or negative ways. Sexual health education programs should facilitate the development of media and digital literacy skills that will enable people to critically evaluate the sexuality-related material they encounter, as well as develop the knowledge and skills to use communication technologies safely and respectfully . The examination of adolescent sexuality provides an excellent example of how social context shapes our sexual beliefs, attitudes, and behaviours. As noted above, adolescents living in Western culture receive contradictory messages about sexuality. For example, many parents and religious institutions send the message that teens should not be sexually active while peers and the media may send the opposite message. The sexual health messages contained in school-based programs may be contradicted by the sexually explicit imagery easily found on the internet. Thus, its not surprising that many adolescents are confused and anxious about sexuality. Key Point Adolescents living in Western culture receive contradictory messages about sexuality. Increasing attention is being paid to the role that the media, particularly television and music videos, plays in influencing adolescent sexuality. Generally, it is assumed that the media's influence is negative. Consider also that adolescents today have much easier access to sexually explicit media (e.g., x-rated videos or pictures) through the internet than did adolescents in the past. For example, a survey of youth in Canada indicated that 22 in grades 7 to 11 reported looking for pornography online and 32 said that they had unintentionally come across pornography without looking for it (Media Smarts, 2022). 20YCWW 20Phase 20IV.pdf Our culture's ambivalence about the reality of adolescent sexuality, combined with the array of contradictory messages about sexuality that adolescents are exposed to, underscores the need to provide effective sexual health education to youth. Part 2: Learning Objectives By the end of this part of the module students will be able to: 1. Classify and describe different ideological perspectives towards sexuality education in the schools. 2. Identify and describe Canadian's attitudes towards sexuality education in the schools. 3. Assess adolescent's needs with respect to sexuality education. 4. Identify the key ingredients of effective adolescent sexuality education. Topic Overview Introduction As we saw in Module 1, and throughout the course so far, the social context of human sexuality in Western culture can be examined in terms of the struggle between the Restrictive and Permissive sexual ideologies. Although Western society appears, over time, to be tilting towards Permissive sexual ideology, there are many sexuality issues upon which Canadian society remains divided. The issue of sexuality education in the schools is also a good case study for examining societal attitudes towards sexuality. \"Sex education is potentially a vehicle for social engineering par excellence, be it progressive or traditional\". \"...educators in the field of sexuality inevitably do their work under some assumptions about its purpose and value - assumptions that include a particular vision of the place of sexuality in social behaviour in general and the needs of teenagers in particular\" . In Module 4, we became familiar with the concept of socialization (The ways in which society conveys to the individual its expectations for his or her behaviour). To a great extent, our sexuality related attitudes and behaviours are the result of the socialization process that occurs as we are growing up. Along with families, friends, religious institutions, and the media, schools are among the most powerful socialization agents in our society. It's not surprising then, that opinions about what should be taught in school-based sexuality education will be a reflection of different ideological perspectives towards sexuality generally. Key Point Schools are one of the primary mechanisms for the socialization of youth in our society and, as a result, sexuality education in the schools is often perceived as a powerful force in shaping the sexuality attitudes and values of youth. Ideology and Sexuality Education: Different Perspectives Restrictive Sexual Ideology: During the 1970's and 1980's, proponents of Restrictive sexual ideology argued that sexuality education did not belong in the schools. In this view, education about sexuality should be left exclusively to parents and religious institutions. From this perspective, sexuality education in the schools would provoke increased sexual curiosity and behaviour among youth. As it became clear, particularly in the 1990's, that schools would play some role in educating youth about sexuality, proponents of Restrictive sexual ideology tended to modify their position to argue that school-based programs should be focused on the primary objective of teaching youth that sexual activity outside of marriage is immoral, psychologically harmful, and unhealthy. These so-called \"abstinence-only\" programs have been far more popular in the United States than in Canada. Indeed, the U.S. government actively funds and encourages abstinence programs. Legislation signed into law by U.S. President Bill Clinton in 1996 included a provision that in order to receive federal funding, sexuality education programs must teach \"...that a mutually monogamous relationship in the context of marriage is the expected standard of human sexual activity\" and \"...that sexual activity outside the context of marriage is likely to have harmful psychological and physical effects\" (cited in Daley, 1997, ). Permissive Sexual Ideology: During the 1970's and 1980's, proponents of Permissive sexual ideology argued that sexuality education did belong in the schools. From this perspective, sexuality education in the schools would help to reduce sexuality related social problems such as teen pregnancy and HIV STI. In this view, knowledge was preferable to ignorance and youth should be taught that sexuality is a natural and positive part of life. Students would be encouraged to clarify their own values about the appropriateness of premarital sex and they would also be informed about birth control methods and ways to reduce the risks of sexual activity (e.g., condom use). Although many school-based sexuality education programs in Canada today make a point of stressing the advantages of abstinence, most programs, particularly in non-religious public schools, do acknowledge the importance of dual protection against pregnancy and HIV STD for sexually active youth. A Democratic Approach to Sexuality Education: Is it possible for sexuality education in the schools to avoid indoctrinating youth with a particular sexual ideology? In one respect, it seems clear that as Canadian society has, in some respects, adopted a more Permissive sexual ideology, these shifts in social attitudes have been reflected in our approaches to teaching youth about sexuality. For example, teaching that using condoms is a wise choice for sexually active youth or including the sexual health education needs of LGBTQI2S students in school curricula can be seen as examples of sexuality education being informed by Permissive sexual ideology. On the other hand, many sexuality educators and policy makers, particularly in Canada, have suggested a philosophical approach to sexuality education that is based, first and foremost, not in either Restrictive or Permissive sexual ideology, but rather on the basic principles of a democratic society. As noted above, the U.S. government unambiguously sides with Restrictive sexual ideology by funding and promoting abstinence-only sex education. Although in Canada, education is a provincial responsibility, the Canadian federal government has played a role in the past in sexuality education. A notable example of this was the Public Health Agency of Canada's Canadian Guidelines for Sexual Health Education which took a quite different approach than the stance taken by the U.S. government. Consider the following statements from those Canadian guidelines. The Guidelines stateed that effective sexual health education: \"is structured so that changes in behaviour and confidence is developed as a result of nonjudgemental and informed decision-making\" (). \"should be provided in an age-appropriate, culturally sensitive manner that is respectful of individual sexual diversity, abilities and choices\" (). In sum, it would appear that, in contrast to U.S. policy, Canadian approaches to sexuality education reflect basic democratic principles such as the right to self-determination and the right to receive information that enables people to make their own choices. For a more modern version of these principles see the Core Principles of Comprehensive Sexual Health Education from the 2019 edition of the Canadian Guidelines for Sexual Health Education: Before examining Canadian's attitudes towards sexuality education in schools, lets take a very quick look at the history of school-based sexuality education in Canada and briefly evaluate the quality of current sex education programs. A Brief History of School-based Sexuality Education in Canada Up until the 1970's, there were few debates about sexuality education in the schools, largely because few schools had sexuality education programs. Students sometimes received limited information about reproduction and sexually transmitted diseases through lectures on \"personal hygiene\", or through biology and physical education classes. Beginning in the 1970's, concern about teenage pregnancies combined with increasing societal openness about sexuality led to the gradual implementation of sexuality education programs in Canadian schools. In the 1980's and 1990's, alarm over HIV AIDS, high rates of other sexually transmitted infections in youth, as well as a growing recognition that most Canadian youth were becoming sexually active in their teens, prompted most secondary schools in Canada to introduce some form of sexuality education. By the mid-1990's, every province and territory in Canada either mandated or strongly recommended, through provincial departments of education or health, that some form of sexuality education be taught in the schools . More recently, the province of Quebec has removed sexual health education from its formal curriculum although the Quebec Ministry of Education recommends that teachers find ways to integrate sexual health issues into classroom teaching. Key Point Every province and territory in Canada either mandates or strongly recommends that some form of sexuality education be taught in the schools. The Current Status of Sexuality Education in Canadian Schools What can we say about the current status of sexuality education in Canadian schools? Although it would be accurate to say that most Canadian youth receive some form of sexuality education before they leave high school, it is also true that few Canadian youth receive sexuality education that provides them with the information and skills necessary to protect and enhance their sexual health. Key Point Although most Canadian youth receive some form of sexuality education before leaving high school, few of these programs provide the necessary information, motivation, and behavioural skills that youth need to protect and enhance their sexual health. The quality of sexuality education in Canadian schools varies from school to school, from school board to school board and from province to province. Thus, it is difficult to generalize about the quality of sexuality education in Canadian schools. However, a number of observations can be made that suggest that there are many weaknesses in contemporary sexuality education. 1. According to data from the Canadian Community Health Survey (Rotermann, 2012; SIECCAN, 2020), about 9 of youth have intercourse before age 15 and another 26 have intercourse at 15 or 16. Yet, many, if not most Canadian youth do not receive detailed education on birth control and condom use until the later grades of high school. In other words, by the time they receive sexuality education, many youth have already become sexually active. 2. Sexual health education programs for adolescents tend to focus primarily on the prevention of sexual problems such as STIs but pay little attention to the enhancement of sexual health and well-being (e.g., healthy, mutually satisfying and pleasurable relationships). 3. Many sexuality education programs in Canadian schools focus on providing basic factual information on the biological aspects of human sexuality. As we will see below, simply providing youth with information on the biological aspects of human sexuality is unlikely, by itself, to result in youth adopting behavioural practices to protect and enhance their sexual health. 4. Very few school teachers have been given specific training on how to provide effective sexuality education programs. 5. Many school principles and administrators believe that providing sexuality education in the schools is highly controversial. They are, therefore, often reluctant to have topics such as sexual orientation and condom use included in the curriculum out of fear that many parents will object to these topics being taught. Catholic schools, in particular, are often reluctant to teach these topics. Canadian Attitudes Towards Sexuality Education As noted above, there is a common perception that sexuality education in the schools is a controversial topic and that many parents strongly object to the idea that their children will be taught about topics such as sexual orientation and condom use. To what extent is this true? Some parents do object to these topics being taught because they do not want the schools to contradict the religious or ethnocultural values related to sexuality that they are trying to pass on to their children. However, it is also true that most parents want their children to receive sexuality education in the schools. Key Point A strong majority of parents approve of sexuality education in the schools. Not only do most Canadian parents want sexuality education taught in the schools, parents also want these programs to teach a broad range of topics. Surveys of parents in Canada have found that most parents approve of the teaching of a wide range of topics including healthy relationships, sexual pleasure, masturbation, methods of STI prevention, birth control, gender identity, and sexual orientation (McKay ., 2014; SIECCAN, 2020; Wood ., 2021). Most Canadian parents appear to recognize the importance of providing youth with broadly-based sexuality education that addresses the realities of adolescent sexuality and sexual behaviour. Not surprisingly, surveys of Canadian youth clearly show that they want relevant sexual health education provided in their schools . However, these same studies also show that few students are satisfied with the sexual health education they are currently receiving . Here is a recent assessment from youth in Canada on their sexual health education experiences and needs: Working Towards Effective Sexuality Education in the Schools In your required reading for this module you will learn about the characteristics of effective sexuality education programs. Among the most important characteristics of effective programs is that they use theoretical models of behaviour change to create and teach the program. Key Point Effective sexuality education programs are informed by theoretical models of behaviour change. The Canadian Guidelines for Sexual Health Education demonstrate the Information, Motivation, Behavioural Skills theoretical model and we will use the IMB model here to illustrate the principles of effective sexuality education. For more information on the key ingredients of effective school-based sexual health education programs see the SIECCAN document Questions and Answers: Sexual Health Education in Schools and Other Settings. (Both of these document are available online at the SIECCAN website Traditionally, and in many cases today, sexuality education programs focus on providing students with factual information. For example, students might learn that condoms reduce the risk of HIV STI infection or that not having intercourse means that you don't have to worry about pregnancy. But does simply learning this kind of factual information translate into healthy behaviour? Research has consistently shown that learning factual information is not enough. Students must also be motivated to use the information they have learned and they must also learn the actual skills to incorporate the information into their behaviour. Let's look at two examples (obtaining discussing partner consent to sexual activity, using condoms, dental dams, or other barriers to prevent STI transmission) of how the IMB model can be used to formulate effective sexuality education for adolescents. Both of these examples are excerpted from the Canadian Guidelines for Sexual Health Education . Indeed, surveys of students indicate that they want sexuality education to include topics such as \"building equal romantic relationships\", \"sexual decision- making in dating relationships\", \"dealing with peer pressure to be sexually active\", and \"communicating about sex\" . Key Point In order to effectively contribute to adolescent sexual health, sexuality education programs must include a focus on the development of relationship and communication skills. The Bureaucracy The municipal administration is the second component in the machinery of local government. Often referred to as the bureaucracy, this group includes all municipal staff and senior officials who are employed by the municipality. Kernaghan and Siegel define bureaucracy as a form of organization characterized by hierarchical structure, unity of command, hiring and promotion by merit, and specialization of labour . The term bureaucracy can sometimes have a negative connotation that brings to mind images about inefficient public sector employees. It is, however, based on sound principles of public administration and was introduced in an effort to establish fair and consistent decision-making and service and an emphasis on effectiveness. As Tindal . note, there have traditionally been requirements for the establishment of certain statutory officers of the municipality such as treasurer, clerk, or solicitor . While this has been changing over time and there is significant variation across the country, municipalities tend to have some designated, statutory positions. Municipalities are organized based on five basic models of municipal administration: 1. the departmental model, 2. the commissioner or board of management model, 3. the council-manager model, 4. the manager model, and 5. the city manager model. : Early Models Departmental and Board of Management The relationship between council, the administration, and special purpose bodies has evolved over time. The first period of development was from WWII to the 1970s and was characterized by a high degree of integration between municipal councils and the administration. The departmental model and board of management system were prevalent. Special purpose bodies were generally unquestioned. Departmental Model The departmental model was prominent in Canadian municipalities until the mid-1970s. functions and assigned responsibility for a function to an administrative department head. All department heads reported directly to the municipal council, often through a standing committee. Department heads were equal, and each had an independent relationship with the municipal council. Not surprisingly, the model had the tendency to promote the development of bureaucratic empires within departments. Coordination between departments was weak and there was little incentive to integrate policies or services. Commissioner or Board of Management Model The commissioner or board of management model assigns responsibility for the management of the municipality s affairs to a group or board rather than a single city manager. Each commissioner would have responsibility for a group of services for example, all hard services, soft services, corporate administrative services, etc. The group of commissioners, led by the chief administrative officer as a first among equals, would meet regularly to plan and coordinate the operations and management of the municipality. In the past, the mayor may have participated on the board of commissioners or board of management, providing a political- administrative link. 1970s Onward Shifting Models of Administration from the 1970s Onward By the mid-1970s and into the 1980s there was a shift to CAO and city manager models in larger cities. This changed the relationship between senior staff and elected representatives and between departments, which were under pressure to become more administratively integrated and work horizontally across boundaries. In some areas, there was a questioning of the role of special purpose bodies. The 1990s were a time of re-examination in local government that included looking at who does what, examining how it is done, as well as measuring and reorganizing in an effort to find cost savings and efficiencies. Both of these periods of change were influenced by business approaches and principles. There was a sense that governments in general, and local government in particular, were getting too large, were inefficient in delivering services, and had weak internal controls. Tindal . discuss the influence of new public management in local government in Canada and its influence on the organization of local governments. The emphasis on performance and accountability sets these NPM reforms apart from earlier structural changes, and the use of special purpose bodies and board of management and city manager terminology reinforce the desire for more control over government. Municipalities have continued to adapt to ongoing fiscal, downloading, and political pressures by restructuring and refocusing. In general, there has been a reduction in the number of senior officials in municipalities and an emphasis on integration and horizontal linkages within program areas. Municipal administrations are becoming more dynamic, and new approaches to managing issues are being implemented, including service clusters and project teams that involve internal and external stakeholders. Council-Manager Model The council-manager model, popular in the U.S., shifted power from department heads to a strong, central city manager (also called CAO). In this model, the city manager is the only point of contact for the administration with the elected council. Councils in the city-manager system do not usually have standing committees and there is little no interaction between senior staff and councillors. The manager has authority to hire and fire senior staff and exercises strong control over the administration. The city manager also has significant influence over the council, which does not generally have strong operational or program knowledge. While the city manager or CAO is very powerful, they are also very vulnerable, especially in situations of conflict. Sancton notes that there is no Canadian municipality where the full city manager CAO model has been implemented. Many municipalities were reluctant to move to the city manager model because of a fear that the city manager position would be too powerful both in the internal administrative side of the organization and politically in terms of challenges and rivalries with the mayor and members of council. However, Canadian municipalities faced pressures for greater professionalization and a stronger non-political role in managing the municipality. Thus, a modified manager model has become popular. A professional city manager would oversee all administrative activities and departmental functions and report to the municipal council. While the department heads report to the city manager, they also connect with the council through a standing committee structure and have accountability to council through that committee. Council is responsible for hiring the manager and is generally involved in some way in the appointment of senior staff. Chief Administrative Officer Model The chief administrative officer model is a weak or modified form of the city manager model. The CAO would have responsibility for all the administrative areas in the municipality, including finance, clerks, communications, human resources, and legal, but generally, they did not have responsibility for the operating departments that provide services directly to the public. In this model, these departments, such as parks and recreation, transportation, and social services, would be run by a department head or commissioner who would report directly The CAO would not have responsibility or authority for the major services provided by the municipality. City Manager Model In the city manager model, the most senior municipal staff position is the city manager who has responsibility for all municipal administration and service delivery. The city manager reports directly to council. Many authors, including the authors of the course textbook, will use city manager and chief administrative officer interchangeably. It is important to note that there was and still remains a difference in the roles and scope of authority in some municipalities. Preferred Administration Model Today Most municipalities use some form of the city manager or chief administrative officer. This super-bureaucrat plays a key role in the municipal administration and is usually selected and appointed under contract by the municipal council. what the municipality is looking for in its recruitment for a new CAO. Depending on the individual, they may have different types of relationships with the senior staff department heads. Plunkett (as referenced in Tindal ., 2017, 257) describes three types of relationships: Passive the city manager plays a passive role, coordinating and supporting department heads Dominant the manager plays a dominant role, managing and controlling operations and budgets and policy and program recommendations to council Active active relationships are the third type of relationship and are the most common. The city manager will be actively involved with departments in working toward shared priorities and managing the relationship with council. The city manager or CAO has a tough job navigating between the political and administrative and faces high expectations. As described by Canadian CAOs: The CAO is the conduit between governance and employees having that sensibility around making the politics work and the business work. (StrategyCorp, 2019, 53) Being a CAO is about knowing how to live in the political world while keeping one foot firmly in the administrative world. (StrategyCorp, 2018, 36) Municipal issues are complex and interconnected, and there is constant pressure for both innovation and efficiency. Municipalities provide services directly, but they also must manage services that are contracted out or delivered through private-public partnerships or other partnership arrangements. The municipal environment is dynamic because there are multiple stakeholders with competing interests, including the public, property owners (and taxpayers), businesses, developers, nonprofits and charities, the province or territory, and the federal government. Expectations are high. Bureaucratic Influence Bureaucrats are expected to be unbiased, objective, and nonpartisan. Nonetheless, by virtue of their position, expertise, and experience, they exert varying degrees of influence on what municipal government does and how it is done. Senior officials have the most significant influence. While elected members of council vote on policies and programs, the senior bureaucrat plays a critical role in advising the members and implementing their decisions. reports to the standing committees (and sometimes directly to council) about issues, programs, funding, or new policies. Sometimes they are asked by these committees or by council to prepare a report on an issue; other times, they take the initiative and propose a new program or policy or a change to an existing policy. They answer questions, provide information at the committee meeting, and explain why they feel the item should be approved. Once a decision has been made, they are responsible for implementing the decision. There is usually some discretion involved in implementation or policy enforcement, and the senior staff can influence the implementation. Elected councillors rely heavily on senior staff. Councillors are often part-time and rarely have the background, education, or experience in the service areas. They are responsible for a wide range of services they cannot be experts in all the service areas and they come to rely on the knowledgeable and experienced senior staff for advice and direction. Often senior staff have an opinion or perspective on the issue, and their advice is influenced by their staff s perspective on the issue. The non-parliamentary nature of council politics reinforces the influence of the bureaucracy. Political parties usually develop position statements on key policy issues these statements guide the politicians while in office. When they are elected, their platform provides guidance to the bureaucrats concerning priorities and policy directions. As previously discussed, there is no formal party politics at the municipal level, and the municipal election does not create a clear mandate for staff to follow. This discussion is not meant to suggest that senior bureaucrats run the show at municipal council. Rather, it is to illustrate their influence on the machinery of local government and decision-making processes. Accountability Structures and Officers Municipalities may also include one or more independent accountability officers. These roles have been added by municipal councils over the last 20 years as independent officers reporting directly to council. While these officers are employees of the municipality, they are not part of the bureaucracy or administration. They instead focus on distinct functions related to accountability integrity; ethics; complaints; lobbying; stewardship of resources; and open, accessible decision-making. A municipal government must act in the best interest of its community members. councillors are elected by voters and are accountable and responsive to them. But elections are every four years, and accountability is muddied by factors such as poor memory; lack of information; fragmented service and funding structures and program partnerships; and contracting out. We will explore issues of municipal accountability later in the Module 10 discussion of municipal relationships with the public. In addition to accountability through elections, some provinces and territories have provided the option in provincial municipal acts for municipalities to pass bylaws to add formal accountability functions to their municipality. For example, the 2 Ontario Municipal Act gave municipalities the authority to appoint accountability officers. In other cases, provinces have required municipalities to add or arrange for specific accountability functions. Some of the specific accountability functions are described in the following tabs and include: : Integrity Commissioner Integrity commissioners are concerned with the ethical behaviour of elected councillors and the mayor, administer the code of conduct, and provide advice to members of council about potential conflict of interest or ethical issues. Integrity commissioners have authority over municipal councils and municipal agencies, boards, and commissions. Did You Know? Toronto created the first full-time municipal integrity commissioner in 2004 following the Bellamy Inquiry into a computer leasing scandal, which is discussed in the readings for this week. Calgary appointed an integrity commissioner in 2016 with dual integrity and ethics advisory responsibility. A municipal ombudsman is an independent officer who reviews actions and decisions taken by municipal councils and their agencies, boards, and commissions. Ombudsman functions have authority to investigate complaints from the public and to initiate investigations when they feel they are warranted. The exceptions are policy decisions and financial matters (which are the responsibility of the auditor general). The City of Montreal established an ombudsman in 2002. Ontario municipalities can establish their own independent officers or choose to be covered by the Ontario ombudsman. The Ontario ombudsman has authority to review decisions of municipal ombudspersons, except for those of the Toronto officer. Halifax, Winnipeg, and Vancouver are required to have ombudsman functions by their respective provincial legislation. Auditor General A municipal auditor general is different from the internally focused municipal auditor that is part of the municipal administration and reports through a committee of council. The independent auditor general reports directly to council and helps municipal councils be accountable for the stewardship of public funds and resources. Toronto is the only Ontario municipality required, in the 2 City of Toronto Act, to have an independent auditor general. Some municipalities have moved to integrate the auditor general and internal audit functions: Winnipeg changed the responsibilities for their auditor general to include internal audit functions in 2009 as have Hamilton, Calgary, and Edmonton. British Columbia appointed a provincial auditor general in 2012 to provide the independent review function for municipalities in that province. Lobbyist Registrar Registration A lobbyist registration system requires lobbyists to register with the municipality and to comply with municipal rules, processes, and codes of conduct. Lobbyists generally must register each interaction with municipal representatives, identifying who they lobbied and why. The cities of Toronto and Hamilton have independent lobbyist registrars with responsibility for administering the process. When it was set up, Toronto s lobbyist registration was voluntary, but it was subsequently changed to mandatory. The City of Ottawa has combined the integrity commissioner and lobbyist registrar function. The City of Winnipeg originally established an integrity commissioner but expanded the role to include lobbyist registrar before the first official was appointed in early 2017. Closed Meeting Investigator Municipal acts use terms like open, transparent, and accountable to describe municipal decision-making processes. This legislation sets out strict parameters for municipalities to meet in camera in meetings that are closed to the public. The closed meeting investigator reviews municipalities to ensure that they are functioning in accordance with the closed meeting rules. The British Columbia provincial ombudsman investigates closed municipal meetings; in Ontario, the provincial ombudsman does the same, except for Toronto and Ottawa, which have independent closed meeting investigators. Accountability officers provide advice and make recommendations to municipal councils, who, in turn, have the authority to make decisions on the issues and impose any penalties or sanctions. Accountability officers have limited formal authority, but considerable power to influence public opinion (Sancton, 2017, 1). Their independence and public reports provide valuable information to municipal voters and community members. Pause and Reflect Examine your municipalities website. Does it talk about accountability to the community and voters? Does the municipality have accountability officers? If not, does it provide information for community members about how to access provincial officers who provide oversight on municipal decisions and actions? Is the information easy to find and clearly communicated? Do a bit more digging to learn if your municipality has had issues related to accountability. If so, what role did accountability officers play in investigating and resolving the issue? What Are Special Purpose Bodies and What Do They Do? In addition to municipalities, there are a number of other decision-making service delivery bodies at the municipal level known as special purpose bodies or agencies, boards, and commissions that are part of local government. Tindal . estimate that there are about 8,000 municipal special purpose bodies in Canada that control significant resources. I n many Canadian cities, more than a third of the city s operating budget is handed over to special-purpose bodies every year. (Lucas, 2013, 2) Examples include transit commissions, police services boards, hydro commissions, heritage boards, and conservation authorities. Key Point Special purpose bodies are assigned specific responsibility for a purpose or mandate; their role and powers vary depending on their area of focus. These bodies differ greatly in their role and membership. Some have service delivery responsibility while others have service delivery and policy-making powers. Special purpose bodies generally have jurisdictional boundaries that reflect municipal boundaries or the boundaries of a group of municipalities. They have a degree of autonomy from the municipal government and can be created by municipal bylaw or imposed by a province or territory through legislation. Agencies, boards, and commissions are controlled by independent boards that include elected municipal representatives, municipal appointees, provincial appointees, or a mix of each. Funding arrangements also vary they can t impose taxes and often impose user charges. They may receive significant funding from the municipal government or provincial grants. In some cases the municipality will have authority to approve the agency, board, or commission budget because it is integrated into the municipal budget; in other cases it can either approve or reject (but not adjust) the budget; and in other cases, it has no control over the budget. Why Do We Have Special Purpose Bodies? During the early reform phases (discussed in Module 2), provinces deliberately established municipal special purpose bodies to transfer power away from the municipalities to bodies that were composed of provincial appointees (e.g., the Ontario Railway and Municipal Board established in 1906). This served to undermine local democracy by taking power from locally elected representatives and giving it to provincially appointed individuals. In 1977, John Robarts, previous premier of Ontario, headed up a royal commission reviewing the municipal government in the city of Toronto s two-tier metro system. Robarts wrote: The province exercises control over many local services by delegating the responsibility for them not to councils but to special purpose bodies and further that they appear to be sub- units of provincial administration rather than units of local government administration (Ontario, 1977, 96 and 99). This tension continues with each appointment to a provincially designated municipal special purpose body. Provincially established special purpose bodies still serve to disperse decision-making about municipal services and weaken municipal councils. Municipalities have established special purpose bodies, most recently as part of new public management initiatives to move municipalities out of the business of and position them as policy makers, steering the municipality. Municipalities established new corporations and delegated responsibility to them for programs, and they established new bodies with other municipalities to manage joint programs. Municipal special purpose bodies are established by municipalities to serve municipal interests. Many of these organizations are formally incorporated, like the Toronto Transit Commission , Toronto Community Housing, and the Toronto Zoo. The municipality is the sole shareholder of the organization and sets the terms, conditions, and mandate for the special purpose body. Ontario municipalities have a number of other municipal bodies, established in response to provincial legislation and requirements, that vary in the level of control and influence in the municipality. For example, school boards are directly funded by and accountable to the Ontario government, yet school board representatives are directly elected in municipal elections. Police service boards and public health boards include some municipally elected representatives and appointed citizen members. Police boards also include provincially appointed members. Inter-municipal Agencies, Boards, or Commissions Sometimes municipalities work together to form organizations like the Association of Municipalities of Ontario , the Association of Manitoba Municipalities , or the Federation of Municipalities of Canada . Alternatively, they may collaborate with municipal neighbours by establishing an agency to address issues of joint concern. Provincially Established Municipal Special Purpose Bodies Many special purpose bodies are mandated by the province or territory. This means that there is legislation that assigns responsibility for the service to an agency, board, or commission established by the province or territory. Here are three Ontario-based examples to illustrate different types of provincially established municipal special purpose bodies. : Police Services Boards Ontario In Ontario, the Police Services Act requires the establishment of a police services board in every municipality that has a police force. The legislation describes the role, membership, and appointment of local police services boards. Boards of three, five, or seven members are required, depending on population size. The police services board in Toronto includes the mayor, two councillors, three provincial appointees, and one citizen appointee. The police chief is accountable to the board, and the board is accountable to the community as well as to the Ontario Civilian In 2019, the City of Toronto estimated that the average property owner, with a property tax of 3,020, would contribute 703.21 toward the cost of policing . Even though the City of Toronto has to raise the money to pay for policing through the property tax, they do not direct the police force or set policing policy, with three of seven votes on the police services board. Metrolinx Metrolinx is a provincial agency that was originally established as the Greater Toronto Transit Authority and included members from municipal councils in the Greater Toronto area. The GTTA was changed to Metrolinx in 2006 and given responsibility for regional transportation planning, developing a unified regional transit fare system, procurement, and duties including development and construction related to the regional transportation system. Metrolinx s 15-member board of directors is appointed by the Lieutenant Governor of Ontario on behalf of Ontario. There are no elected members of council from any of the municipalities in the Metrolinx catchment area on the board of directors, even though some of them operate municipal transit programs. The provincial agency makes decisions that have implications for municipal transit operators. For example, Metrolinx is rolling out a common electronic payment system, called Presto, across the partner transit systems. Each transit operator is concerned about a negative impact of this system on their operations. The TTC, Toronto s transit provider, published the results of a study that the TTC had lost revenues of about 4.2 M as a result of the Toronto roll-out of the payment system. In addition, Metrolinx s responsibility for transit planning and decisions about investment in new transit have implications for municipal economic development and growth. Decisions about new GO stations (a regional transit service) or frequency of transit service can influence the shape of municipalities. Metrolinx provides an example of a provincially established ABC that integrates and plans for regions (including municipalities) without decision-making involvement of the elected officials from those municipalities. You have read about the Ontario Municipal Board in earlier modules. Other provinces have similar independent oversight bodies established to monitor and make some decisions related to municipalities. The OMB was established in 1906 as the Ontario Railway and Municipal Board to oversee the finances of municipalities and supervise the railways, which were, at the time, the main source of transport between municipalities. Eventually, the OMB gained more responsibility to adjudicate in cases of dispute related to some regulations, planning, and development. Interestingly, it has retained authority to approve municipal borrowing for capital expenditures for all Ontario municipalities! The OMB was controversial in its role as the appeal body in the case of a dispute over a municipal decision. It was used most frequently to challenge decisions regarding zoning and planning matters, but Module 4 described how a councillor appealed to the OMB regarding the decision on Toronto ward boundaries. In 2018, Ontario replaced the OMB by giving municipalities the authority to establish independent local planning appeal tribunals in accordance with provincial legislation. Toronto set up a Toronto Local Planning Appeal Tribunal to assume some of the functions previously provided by the OMB, including appeals on a range of planning and land matters. In 2019, Ontario announced changes to the LPAT process instead of referring appeals back to the municipality for further consideration if the tribunal disagreed with the municipal decision, the LPAT would have the authority to make the final and binding decision. In effect, they were given the powers of the old OMB, which led to widespread criticism of that provincial agency. This is a good example of how agencies can be used and adapted based on political interests in this case, based on provincial interests. Are Special Purpose Bodies Good for Local Government? There is considerable debate whether special purpose bodies are good for local government. Supporters argue that some services, such as policing, may be too sensitive to leave in the hands of elected officials and they appreciate the mixed board structure that includes at least one community representative. Others support the focus and attention to a service area or issue given by a special purpose body and to the assignment of responsibility to appointees with expertise and knowledge of the issue area. Municipalities have wide and broad responsibility. Assigning some of that responsibility to a special purpose agency will bring attention and clear focus to that service and, at the same time, will give municipal councils more time and energy to address their core functions. The result may be more effective and more efficient service delivery. Critics counter that it is undemocratic to take power from elected officials who have been chosen by the public to represent them and assign it to appointed individuals with no direct accountability. Unelected special purpose bodies may not be responsive to public concerns. The existence of so many bodies can lead to confusion among residents about how local government works. Transparency in decision-making processes may vary among municipal agencies, contributing to confusion and concerns about accountability. Similar questions of accountability can be directed to the composition of the boards. Should they include elected or appointed members or both? What about provincial boards established in municipal areas should they include municipal representatives, either elected or appointed? Accountability is also important in funding. Municipalities contribute to many agencies, boards, and commissions but don t always have a say in how the resources are used. Provincially established municipal agencies bring additional benefits and challenges. If the agency crosses municipal boundaries, it has potential to bring attention and leadership to a shared issue of concern. It is possible that a provincially established municipal agency will have access to provincial funds that otherwise wouldn t have been available. Moreover, in situations where there is conflict among municipalities, a provincially established municipal agency may be able to negotiate a resolution. Provincial special purpose bodies are often seen to be a way of weakening local councils and extending provincial control This happens through the establishment of the agency and in the ongoing appointment of provincial nominees to the board of the special purpose body. There is no local accountability for the actions of provincial municipal agencies the accountability is to the province. Community members, confused by municipal agencies and the municipality, will be further confused by the existence of provincially established agencies at the municipal level. As the examples showed, there is potential for conflict and tension about political agendas and priorities and funding. Provincially established municipal agencies reduce scope for municipal decision-making autonomy John Robarts, quoted earlier, recommended that all special purpose bodies be abolished and that responsibility for the issue areas should be given back to municipalities. Pause and Reflect Look again at your municipal website. Does the website identify any municipally established special purpose bodies? If so, what do they do and how do they connect with the municipality? Are there some agencies, boards, and commissions that you know about that aren t listed on the website? Why? What about provincial special purpose bodies? Is there information on the municipal website about them? If not, is it easy to identify them and learn more? Finally, do you think there are more advantages or disadvantages to having municipal special purpose bodies? What about provincially established municipal agencies, boards, and commissions are you pro or con? Summary This module completes our look at the machinery of local government. It showed that municipal councils may be the elected decision-makers in local government, but agencies, boards, and commissions also make important decisions about key municipal services and programs. The module distinguished between municipally and provincially established special purpose bodies that are active at the municipal level and considered the implications for municipal authority and autonomy. Staff support informed decision-making and implement directions from council they too play an important role in shaping and influencing decisions and implementation. The different administrative models show different relationships between senior staff and municipal councils, with implications for authority and influence. The module introduced accountability officers senior staff appointed directly by municipal council who report directly to council. These accountability officers are independent municipal employees and are not part of the administration. Not all municipalities have these functions, but many are covered by officers providing some of the functions at the provincial or territorial level. The machinery of local government is complex and dynamic. It changes over time based on events and actions, our understanding of local government, and the relationships between the elected representatives, the administration, and the agencies, boards, and commissions. The assignment Municipal Decision-Making due at the end of this course week will give you the opportunity to further reflect on the machinery of local government. The municipal administration is a key element of the machinery of local government. The administrative models have evolved over time based on a number of pressures, including the relationship with council. Most municipalities follow a city manager (or CAO) model. The city manager plays an important leadership role in the municipality, straddling the political and administrative and juggling a range of challenging issues. Municipal accountability functions include integrity commissioners, municipal ombudspersons, auditor generals, lobbyist registrars, and closed meeting investigators. These may be internal to the municipality, reporting directly to council and separate from municipal administrations, or provided by the province or territory for all municipalities. Municipal agencies, boards, and commissions play important roles in delivering a range of local services and programs. They can be established by the municipality or by a province or territory to cover one or more municipalities. While there are clear benefits to special purpose bodies, there are also some important challenges related to accountability, transparency, and autonomy. The Machinery of Municipal Government Before venturing into the larger and less distinct world of local gover- nance, let s begin with the machinery of local government. More spe- cifically, we will examine the machinery of municipal government not including the structures that may be found amongst the wide variety of agencies, boards, and commissions that form part of local government. On the surface, this approach sounds quite straightforward, and the basic structure of municipal government is certainly simpler than that found at the provincial and federal levels, with their separate executive and legislative branches. There aren t separate branches of government at the municipal level; responsibilities are concentrated in the elected council and are carried out by appointed staff who are mostly organized into a number of functionally specialized departments. he powers assigned to a municipality are exercised on behalf of its resi- dents and ratepayers by a council elected by them. Provincial legislation usually includes provisions for the form of council and such details as the number of councillors and whether election is by general vote (at-large) or by ward (a distinction discussed below). legislation passed in most provinces over the past decade (and discussed in Chapter 6) often gives municipalities somewhat more discretion with respect to such matters. Municipal councils consist of a head (known as warden or chair in counties and other upper-tier governments; mayor in cities and towns; and reeve, chair, or overseer in villages and townships) and a widely varying number of councillors. While the total membership varies greatly, there has been a tendency to have small councils of from 5 to 15 members, largely on the grounds that a small group is less unwieldy and more efficient in making decisions with the more recent exceptions being amalgamated megacities such as Toronto. Members of council are expected to represent the local community and act on its behalf although that role is not nearly as simple or straightforward as it sounds, as discussed below. They also exercise a policy-making role through which they determine services and service levels, approve budgets, enact rules and regulations, and generally shape the local community and the quality of life within it. A third general role of councillors is managerial (for want of a better term), and it involves Chapter 8 Municipal Governing Structures 227 providing an oversight of municipal operations to ensure that policies are implemented as intended, funds are expended as authorized, and pro- grams are delivered efficiently and effectively. This local politician civic staff relationship is sometimes a bit more nuanced, with suggestions that permanent professional staff can at times have more policy sway than is generally understood.5 THE REPRESENTATIVE ROLE OF MEMBERS OF COUNCIL The roles of councillors in making policy and overseeing implementation of policy by municipal staff receive a good deal of emphasis and will be explored in a subsequent section on council-staff relations. But it is a con- sistent theme of this text that the representative role of municipal govern- ment is most important, and it is the elected members of council who fulfill this role, well or poorly. The longstanding bias in favour of small councils makes it more likely that they will not represent adequately the diversity of the population. Relatively small councils are even found in many of Canada s largest municipalities. While First Nations, M tis, and Inuit are legally recognized as Aboriginal in the Constitution Act, 1982, this wasn t always the case. There were past legal distinctions between the three groups and for many years Indian peoples were the only peoples formally recognized in the Constitution. A Supreme Court ruling in 1929 recognized Inuit peoples as covered by the Constitution Act, 1987 (OECD, 2020, 44). M tis were legally recognized for the first time in the Constitution Act, 1982 (OECD, 2020, 44). It is important to note that there are also legal distinctions set out in the Indian Act, between registered status Indians and non-status Indians. Key Point You will notice that different terms are used to describe Indigenous people. Efforts have been made to use the terms used by a specific researcher when referencing their research or terms used in legislation. For example, you will see reference to Indian (terminology used in the past by the federal government) and to Aboriginal peoples (the term used currently by the federal government). First Nations, M tis, and Inuit are used where appropriate to refer to specific peoples. Unless designated by a source, the module will use the term Indigenous peoples analogous to the term European to refer to the descendants of all the original nations and peoples of Canada (OECD, 2020, 39).
